question: A home care nurse is helping a diabetic patient manage blood sugar using local Nigerian foods. What is the best approach?

options.A: Insist the patient only eat imported foods recommended in standard textbooks
options.B: Tell the patient to stop eating altogether until blood sugar normalizes
options.C: Ignore the diabetes and let the patient eat whatever they want
options.D: Adapt the diabetic meal plan using accessible local staples and traditional foods

explanation: Brilliant! Good nursing means working with familiar, local foods so the patient can easily stick to their health plan. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h3)

question: What position should a patient be in during oral feeding to stop them from choking?

options.A: Slumped forward with the chin touching the chest
options.B: Lying flat on their back with one pillow
options.C: Reclining sideways on the left hip
options.D: Sitting upright at a 90-degree angle

explanation: Correct! Sitting upright uses gravity to guide food safely down the food pipe instead of the windpipe. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h4)

question: Which sign strongly suggests a patient is struggling to swallow during a meal?

options.A: Asking for a glass of clean water
options.B: Finishing the meal within ten minutes
options.C: A gurgling voice right after swallowing
options.D: Chewing food slowly on one side

explanation: Spot on! A wet or gurgling voice means food or drink slipped into the upper airway. Good eye spotting that! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h4)

question: Why must a feeding tube be flushed with warm water before and after giving formula?

options.A: To check the patient's blood pressure
options.B: To prevent the tube from clogging
options.C: To hydrate the patient's skin
options.D: To cool down the internal stomach lining

explanation: You got it! Flushing clears out thick formula or crushed meds so the narrow tube doesn't block up. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why is it important to keep the head of the bed raised during a home tube feeding?

options.A: To prevent stomach contents from flowing back into the lungs
options.B: To keep the external tubing straight and secure
options.C: To make it easier for the caregiver to reach the pump
options.D: To help the formula digest faster in the stomach

explanation: Spot on! Elevation uses gravity to keep the liquid formula safely in the stomach, preventing dangerous aspiration. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is a common cause of diarrhea when a patient is receiving tube feeds at home?

options.A: Elevating the bed during the feeding
options.B: Keeping the room temperature too warm
options.C: Infusing the formula too rapidly
options.D: Flushing the tube with plain sterile water

explanation: Correct! Pumping formula too fast overwhelms the gut and frequently causes cramps and diarrhea. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h6)

question: An elderly patient gets too tired halfway through meals and leaves most food. What should you suggest?

options.A: Force the patient to finish everything on the plate
options.B: Serve smaller, more frequent meals throughout the day
options.C: Wait until the patient asks for food days later
options.D: Stop offering solid food and start tube feeding

explanation: Great thinking! Smaller portions prevent fatigue and help weak patients eat enough total calories. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h6)

question: What is the best way to confirm a family caregiver actually knows how to manage a feeding tube?

options.A: Ask if they understood the instructions given
options.B: Give the caregiver a written quiz on medical terms
options.C: Ask the caregiver to demonstrate the skill back to the nurse
options.D: Check if they bought the required equipment

explanation: Spot on! Return demonstration is the gold standard to make sure they can do it safely on their own. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h7)

question: Why is helping with caregiver burnout a vital part of home nutrition management?

options.A: An exhausted caregiver may make dangerous mistakes in patient feeding
options.B: Tired family members usually forget to pay nursing fees
options.C: Caregivers need rest to prevent catching the patient's illness
options.D: Burnout immediately causes the patient's appetite to disappear

explanation: Exactly! When caregivers are completely drained, they are much more likely to make errors with feeds and meds. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h7)

question: Which detail is most important for a home nurse to record during feeding visits?

options.A: Estimated percentage of meals eaten and weight trends
options.B: The exact brand of dishes used in the household
options.C: The grocery store prices of all purchased food
options.D: The names of visiting neighbors and friends

explanation: You got it! Tracking intake percentages and weight changes tells you clearly if the nutrition plan is working. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h8)

question: Why is teamwork between different healthcare pros so important in home nutrition care?

options.A: Doctors require every single discipline to sign off on grocery lists
options.B: It ensures the nurse does not have to visit the patient's home very often
options.C: It prevents family members from participating in meal preparation
options.D: Different specialists bring unique skills like swallowing therapy or diet design to keep the patient safe

explanation: Spot on! Speech therapists handle swallowing, dietitians handle meal plans, and together they keep the patient safe. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T7#GNS324_U3_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary definition of ambulation in healthcare?

options.A: The physical therapy exercise routine
options.B: The ability of a patient to walk
options.C: The safe transfer from bed to chair
options.D: The prevention of blood clots in legs

explanation: Ambulation simply means walking, whether done completely on one's own or with the help of a device or another person. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Why is maintaining a patient's mobility considered vital for overall health?

options.A: It shortens the required hospital stay to one day
options.B: It guarantees complete recovery from any surgery
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for pain medication
options.D: It supports circulation and preserves muscle mass

explanation: Movement keeps blood flowing properly and prevents muscles from weakening quickly during illness or recovery. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which body systems work together to create coordinated movement?

options.A: Musculoskeletal and nervous systems
options.B: Cardiovascular and lymphatic systems
options.C: Respiratory and endocrine systems
options.D: Digestive and urinary systems

explanation: Movement requires the structural support of bones and muscles directed and coordinated by the nervous system. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary role of skeletal muscles during ambulation?

options.A: Contracting to pull bones and create motion
options.B: Sending electrical signals to the brain
options.C: Producing red blood cells for oxygen transport
options.D: Absorbing shock within the joint spaces

explanation: Skeletal muscles shorten and pull on bones across joints to move the body forward during walking. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is a primary goal of performing a nursing mobility assessment?

options.A: To replace the need for physical therapy input
options.B: To determine functional capacity and plan safe care
options.C: To diagnose underlying genetic bone disorders
options.D: To measure exact daily caloric requirements

explanation: Assessing mobility shows what a patient can safely do on their own and what help they need. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: A patient is asked to stand up from a chair, walk ten feet, turn around, and sit back down. What is this clinical observation called?

options.A: Pulmonary function trial
options.B: Cardiorespiratory stress exam
options.C: Get-Up-and-Go test
options.D: Neurological reflex screen

explanation: The Get-Up-and-Go test is a quick, practical way to evaluate a patient's balance, sit-to-stand transition, and walking stability. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: On which side of the body should a patient hold a single-point walking cane?

options.A: Alternating hands with every step
options.B: Always in the dominant hand
options.C: The weak side of the body
options.D: The strong side of the body

explanation: Holding the cane on the strong side allows the patient to lean weight onto the device while moving the weaker leg forward. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: A patient using axillary crutches complains of numbness and tingling in their fingers. What instruction should the nurse provide?

options.A: Switch immediately to using a standard four-wheeled walker
options.B: Adjust the crutches so they fit higher up in the armpit
options.C: Lean your upper body forward to relieve hand pressure
options.D: Support your body weight on your hands, not your armpits

explanation: Resting body weight on the armpits compresses nerves and blood vessels, leading to nerve damage and tingling; weight must go through the hand grips. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary safety item a nurse should place around a patient's waist before assisting with a transfer?

options.A: A standard leather belt
options.B: A soft restraining strap
options.C: A gait belt
options.D: An elastic binder

explanation: A gait belt gives the nurse a safe, secure handhold to support the patient without pulling on their clothing or arms. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to keep a wide stance and bend their knees when lifting or moving a patient?

options.A: To increase upper body muscular strength instantly
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nervous or unsteady
options.C: To ensure the patient can place their feet flat on the floor
options.D: To lower the center of gravity and protect the back

explanation: Proper body mechanics with a wide base of support reduces strain on the nurse's lumbar spine during physical maneuvers. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: How often should a bedbound patient ideally be repositioned to prevent pressure injuries?

options.A: Only when the patient complains
options.B: Once every twelve hours
options.C: At least every two hours
options.D: Once per day during the morning shift

explanation: Turning or repositioning a patient every two hours relieves continuous pressure on vulnerable skin areas and tissues. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which complication is most directly linked to sluggish blood flow in the legs of an immobile patient?

options.A: Orthostatic hypotension
options.B: Deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Immobility slows venous return from the lower extremities, which allows blood clots to form more easily in deep veins. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which of the following is a common home hazard that frequently leads to patient falls?

options.A: Bright lighting in bedroom hallways
options.B: Grab bars installed inside showers
options.C: Low-pile wall-to-wall carpeting
options.D: Loose scatter rugs on slick floors

explanation: Loose rugs easily slip underfoot or catch assistive device tips, making them a major tripping hazard in homes. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: A patient with unsteady balance prepares for discharge home. What is the best nursing action to address home safety?

options.A: Discuss removing tripping hazards and installing bathroom grab bars
options.B: Advise the patient to remain in bed until fully recovered
options.C: Recommend replacing all furniture with hospital-grade equipment
options.D: Suggest wearing thick socks for warmth and comfort while walking

explanation: Practical modifications like clearing walkways and adding bathroom grab bars directly prevent falls in the living environment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: Why is visiting a patient's home so helpful for disease management?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any medications.
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will never need a hospital visit.
options.C: It allows nurses to observe real-world habits and living conditions.
options.D: It places the entire workload on family members instead.

explanation: You get a true picture when you see where patients actually live! Home care lets you spot daily habits and environmental factors that directly affect their health. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: How does home care primarily change the way healthcare is delivered?

options.A: From hospital-centered interventions to daily life
options.B: From professional nursing to family-only treatment
options.C: From chronic disease management to acute surgery
options.D: From everyday living to rigid facility schedules

explanation: Instead of keeping care locked inside hospital walls, home nursing brings support directly into the patient's personal living space. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which of these is a great example of primary prevention in the home?

options.A: Performing range-of-motion exercises for a stroke survivor
options.B: Checking blood sugar levels to find early diabetes
options.C: Giving a seasonal flu vaccine to a healthy client
options.D: Treating an open pressure ulcer on the heel

explanation: Primary prevention stops illnesses before they even start. Giving a vaccine to a healthy person is a classic way to protect them! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention?

options.A: To reduce complications and manage established chronic illnesses
options.B: To prevent a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person
options.C: To screen a population for hidden risk factors
options.D: To cure acute infections using high-dose antibiotics

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a disease is already there—helping patients manage symptoms, avoid complications, and live their best daily life. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h2)

question: When checking a home for safety, which of these is a common physical hazard?

options.A: High white blood cell count
options.B: Elevated resting heart rate
options.C: Incorrect medication dosage
options.D: Loose floor rugs

explanation: Watch out for loose rugs! They are physical hazards that easily cause elderly patients to trip and fall at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: A nurse notices a dark hallway and no grab bars in the shower. What type of assessment is this?

options.A: Home environmental safety assessment
options.B: Pharmacological toxicity review
options.C: Tertiary rehabilitation evaluation
options.D: Secondary disease screening

explanation: Spotting physical risks like poor lighting or missing bathroom grab bars is part of a home environmental safety check. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h3)

question: What daily measurement is most crucial for a home care patient with heart failure?

options.A: Handgrip strength
options.B: Visual acuity
options.C: Body weight
options.D: Hair growth rate

explanation: Daily weighing is a lifesaver for heart failure patients. It helps catch hidden fluid buildup early before serious breathing problems start. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h4)

question: Why is teaching patients to spot early warning signs of their chronic disease so important?

options.A: It completely cures chronic conditions like diabetes.
options.B: It ensures family members take over all nursing duties.
options.C: It stops patients from ever taking prescription drugs.
options.D: It allows for early action before emergency hospitalization is needed.

explanation: When patients recognize small changes early, they can call for help or adjust care before a scary health crisis lands them in the hospital. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which handy tool do home care nurses often use to help patients manage multiple daily pills?

options.A: Sterile wound dressing
options.B: Blood pressure cuff
options.C: Peak flow meter
options.D: Weekly pill organizer

explanation: A weekly pill box is a simple lifesaver! It sorts medications by days and times, helping patients stay on track. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: Why do many older home care patients struggle to take their medications correctly?

options.A: They have too many extra financial resources.
options.B: Complex dosing schedules cause confusion.
options.C: Doctors always prescribe only one pill per day.
options.D: Medication bottles are always too easy to open.

explanation: When a patient has too many pills with different rules (some before meals, some at bedtime), it gets super confusing. Keeping it simple is key! [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in home care?

options.A: Proper hand hygiene
options.B: Restricting all visitors permanently
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns all day
options.D: Spraying rooms with strong perfumes

explanation: Good old-fashioned handwashing is your best defense! It removes germs and stops them from passing between you and your patients. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: Which of these is a common myth about infection control in home settings?

options.A: That handwashing helps reduce bacterial spread
options.B: That family members can transmit respiratory viruses
options.C: That the home environment is naturally germ-free
options.D: That used needles require special puncture-proof containers

explanation: Don't be fooled—homes are not naturally sterile! Good cleaning and hygiene habits are still a must everywhere. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is the purpose of using the 'teach-back' method during patient education?

options.A: Asking the patient to repeat instructions in their own words
options.B: Testing the patient on medical history terminology
options.C: Reading a medical textbook aloud to the family
options.D: Having the nurse lecture for an hour without stopping

explanation: Teach-back is brilliant: you ask them to explain your instructions back to you in their own words so you know they truly understand. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: Why should nurses actively involve family caregivers in disease management education?

options.A: It removes all responsibility from the professional nurse.
options.B: It helps caregivers spot red flags and offer safe daily support.
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever speaking to a doctor.
options.D: It ensures the family takes over financial medical costs.

explanation: Family members are with the patient every day. Training them means someone is always watching for warning signs when you aren't there. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h7)

question: Which healthcare professional do home care nurses often team up with to improve patient mobility?

options.A: Hospital security guards
options.B: Pharmaceutical researchers
options.C: Financial accountants
options.D: Physical therapists

explanation: Physical therapists are fantastic partners! They work alongside nurses to help patients build strength, balance, and safely move around at home. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)

question: What is a key part of emergency preparedness in a home care plan?

options.A: Disconnecting all medical equipment to save electricity
options.B: Waiting for the annual checkup to report severe symptoms
options.C: Knowing who to call and what steps to take during a sudden crisis
options.D: Relying solely on neighbors for medical decisions

explanation: When an emergency strikes, panic shouldn't take over. Having a clear plan of who to call keeps both the patient and family safe. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T9#GNS324_U3_T9_h8)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the emotional alarm system that triggers the fight-or-flight response during anxiety?

options.A: The pituitary gland
options.B: The cerebellum
options.C: The medulla oblongata
options.D: The amygdala

explanation: Spot on! The amygdala is our emotional radar. It processes threats and sounds the alarm early when we feel anxious. You've got this! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is the main job of brain chemicals like GABA and serotonin?

options.A: Controlling voluntary skeletal muscle movement
options.B: Managing red blood cell production in bone marrow
options.C: Increasing body temperature during an infection
options.D: Regulating mood and calming nerve activity

explanation: Great job! GABA and serotonin act like natural brakes in the brain, keeping our mood balanced and our nerves from firing too wildly. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h1)

question: To diagnose Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), how long must a patient experience excessive, hard-to-control worry?

options.A: One year
options.B: Six months
options.C: One month
options.D: Two weeks

explanation: Correct! For a GAD diagnosis, the persistent worry needs to span at least six months. Keep up the brilliant study habit! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h2)

question: A patient suddenly feels intense terror, chest pain, and a sense of doom that peaks within minutes. What condition matches this?

options.A: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.B: Social anxiety disorder
options.C: Specific phobia
options.D: Panic disorder

explanation: Exactly! Those sudden, terrifying rushes with strong physical signs are classic hallmarks of panic attacks seen in panic disorder. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h2)

question: How do tough economic pressures and daily security worries affect mental health at home?

options.A: They completely eliminate the biological risk factors for psychiatric illness
options.B: They permanently alter DNA structure within a single generation
options.C: They create chronic, ongoing stress that depletes psychological resilience
options.D: They exclusively cause short-term physical injuries without mental effects

explanation: Spot on! Constant daily stressors keep our nervous system on edge, wearing down our mental strength over time. You're doing great. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a common stressor that can worsen anxiety for people living in Nigeria?

options.A: Economic hardship and inflation
options.B: Security challenges and community unrest
options.C: Societal pressures regarding family provision
options.D: Abundant financial surplus and job security

explanation: That's right! Having plenty of money and job security actually lowers stress rather than causing anxiety. Easy peasy! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h3)

question: Which physical sign do patients very often report when they are feeling extremely anxious?

options.A: Rapid heartbeat or palpitations
options.B: Sustained lowering of blood pressure
options.C: Uncontrolled weight gain over days
options.D: Permanent loss of skin pigmentation

explanation: Correct! When anxiety hits, adrenaline surges through the body, frequently causing a racing heart or palpitations. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h4)

question: Why is it important to run physical medical tests on someone presenting with severe anxiety symptoms?

options.A: To determine the correct dosage of psychotherapy immediately
options.B: To measure the exact concentration of brain neurotransmitters
options.C: To rule out medical conditions like hyperthyroidism that mimic anxiety
options.D: To prove that the patient is faking psychological distress

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like an overactive thyroid can cause a racing pulse and tremors that look just like anxiety. We always check the physical body first! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which group of medications is usually prescribed first for the long-term management of anxiety disorders?

options.A: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
options.B: Short-acting skeletal muscle relaxants
options.C: Intravenous corticosteroid therapies
options.D: First-generation antipsychotic medications

explanation: You got it! SSRIs are the go-to choice for long-term anxiety care because they work well and have a safer side-effect profile. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why are benzodiazepines generally prescribed for short-term use only during sudden, severe anxiety?

options.A: They permanently cure the underlying brain chemistry imbalance in one dose
options.B: They stop working entirely after the very first day of administration
options.C: They carry a significant risk of tolerance and physical dependence
options.D: They immediately cause severe permanent organ damage if used at all

explanation: Spot on! The body gets used to benzodiazepines very quickly, which can lead to dependence and addiction if taken for too long. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h5)

question: A patient is having a rising panic attack at home. What is the best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink several cups of strong coffee
options.B: Scold the patient for worrying over unimportant matters
options.C: Leave the patient completely alone in a dark room until they calm down
options.D: Guide the patient through slow, deep breathing exercises

explanation: Brilliant! Slow, steady breaths help lower the heart rate and calm down hyperventilation. Nursing care at its finest! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h6)

question: How does cutting back on coffee and energy drinks help a patient dealing with an anxiety disorder?

options.A: It prevents central nervous system stimulation that mimics anxiety symptoms
options.B: It guarantees uninterrupted sleep for twelve hours every night
options.C: It acts as a powerful direct replacement for antidepressant medication
options.D: It cures the genetic predisposition linked to panic disorder

explanation: Correct! Caffeine is a stimulant that causes jitteriness and a fast pulse—things you definitely don't need when managing anxiety. Smart choice! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is a frequent risk when people try to self-medicate ongoing, untreated anxiety?

options.A: Substance abuse and dependence
options.B: Sudden permanent loss of vision
options.C: Drastic and rapid skeletal bone growth
options.D: Complete immunity to bacterial infections

explanation: Spot on. Many turn to alcohol or drugs to numb their anxious feelings, which often leads into a struggle with substance dependence. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h7)

question: During a home visit, a patient with severe anxiety mentions thoughts of ending their life. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.A: Tell the patient to snap out of it and focus on positive thoughts
options.B: Wait until the next scheduled clinic appointment in two weeks
options.C: Advise the patient to exercise vigorously until exhausted
options.D: Assess the immediate suicide risk and ensure a safe environment

explanation: You nailed it. Safety always comes first. When a patient talks about self-harm, assessing immediate risk is the most crucial step. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T1#GNS324_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease in the brain?

options.A: Beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles
options.B: Multiple small brain infarctions
options.C: Chronic bacterial infection of the meninges
options.D: Dopamine depletion in the basal ganglia

explanation: Alzheimer's disease is physically characterized by the accumulation of abnormal protein deposits known as beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tau tangles. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why does vascular dementia typically present with a step-wise decline in cognitive function?

options.A: Medications for blood pressure cause sudden memory loss
options.B: Nutritional deficiencies worsen over specific time periods
options.C: Brain damage occurs abruptly with successive strokes
options.D: Tau proteins accumulate in a predictable pattern

explanation: Vascular dementia is driven by cerebrovascular events, meaning cognitive function drops each time a new stroke or ischemic injury occurs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h1)

question: A patient who gets lost in familiar places and needs help with finances is showing signs of which stage?

options.A: Normal aging process
options.B: Late stage dementia
options.C: Delirium secondary to infection
options.D: Early stage dementia

explanation: Getting lost in familiar environments and struggling with complex tasks like finances are classic indicators of early-stage cognitive decline. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h2)

question: A patient with middle-stage dementia accuses family members of stealing personal items. What is the most appropriate understanding of this behavior?

options.A: It is a common behavioral symptom caused by progressive memory loss and confusion
options.B: It indicates the patient has developed acute paranoid schizophrenia
options.C: It proves the family members are actually mishandling the patient's property
options.D: It is a side effect of normal age-related brain shrinkage

explanation: Paranoia and false accusations in middle-stage dementia stem from the brain's inability to make sense of misplaced items or environmental changes. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h2)

question: What is a primary purpose of installing door alarms in the home of a patient with dementia?

options.A: To detect sudden changes in blood pressure
options.B: To monitor daily sleep cycle patterns
options.C: To remind the patient to take medications
options.D: To prevent dangerous wandering behavior

explanation: Wandering is a major safety risk for individuals with dementia, and door alarms alert caregivers before the patient leaves the house unsupervised. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h3)

question: Why is adequate, glare-free lighting especially important in the home environment of a dementia patient?

options.A: It directly stimulates nerve regeneration in the cerebral cortex
options.B: It prevents the patient from experiencing sudden visual hallucinations
options.C: It cures the underlying chemical imbalances causing memory loss
options.D: It reduces visual misinterpretations and shadow-induced paranoia

explanation: Poor lighting creates shadows that patients with altered perception often misinterpret as threatening objects or figures, triggering anxiety and agitation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h3)

question: A patient insists that a deceased spouse is coming home for dinner tonight. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Tell the patient that waiting for the spouse is a waste of time
options.B: Ignore the statement entirely and walk away from the patient without speaking
options.C: Firmly remind the patient that the spouse passed away several years ago
options.D: Gently redirect the conversation to look at a photo album or talk about a favorite meal

explanation: Correcting a patient with dementia causes unnecessary distress and agitation; redirection is a more compassionate and effective communication strategy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h4)

question: What is the most likely meaning behind sudden physical agitation in a non-verbal dementia patient?

options.A: A direct side effect of adequate hydration and proper nutrition
options.B: A deliberate attempt to manipulate family members and caregivers
options.C: An unmet physical need such as pain, hunger, or a full bladder
options.D: A sign that the patient's long-term memory is returning

explanation: Behavioral symptoms are frequently the only way a person with advanced dementia can communicate physical discomfort or basic needs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h4)

question: What is a recommended dietary modification for a patient who forgets how to use cutlery during meals?

options.A: Restricting meals to liquids only
options.B: Serving nutritious finger foods
options.C: Feeding the patient through a syringe
options.D: Administering total parenteral nutrition

explanation: Finger foods allow patients with dementia to feed themselves independently when they lose the ability to manipulate forks and spoons. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h5)

question: Why should caregivers break down dressing into simple, single-step instructions for a patient with moderate dementia?

options.A: It completely reverses the physical weakness in the patient's limbs
options.B: It eliminates the need for any caregiver assistance during hygiene care
options.C: It speeds up the morning routine so the nurse can leave early
options.D: It prevents cognitive overload and preserves residual independence

explanation: Complex multi-step commands overwhelm a damaged brain; breaking tasks down helps the patient process each step successfully. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical goal of prescribing cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil?

options.A: To completely eliminate the need for caregiver supervision
options.B: To temporarily manage cognitive symptoms and improve function
options.C: To reverse existing beta-amyloid brain plaque accumulation
options.D: To permanently cure the underlying neurodegenerative pathology

explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors enhance neurotransmitter availability to provide temporary stabilization of cognitive abilities, though they do not halt the disease process. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h6)

question: Why should antipsychotic medications be used with extreme caution in older adults with dementia?

options.A: They carry an increased risk of stroke and serious adverse events
options.B: They interfere with the absorption of basic dietary proteins
options.C: They completely eliminate the patient's ability to speak or swallow
options.D: They immediately accelerate the rate of brain tissue regeneration

explanation: Regulatory agencies warn that antipsychotic drugs significantly elevate the risk of mortality and stroke in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is a primary objective of introducing respite care for a family caregiver?

options.A: To punish the family for failing to manage behavioral symptoms
options.B: To train the patient to live completely independently in the community
options.C: To provide temporary relief and prevent caregiver burnout
options.D: To permanently transfer legal custody of the patient away from the family

explanation: Respite care offers short-term relief to family caregivers, giving them necessary time to rest, attend to personal needs, and prevent exhaustion. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h7)

question: Why is caregiver burnout especially prevalent in settings like Nigeria where formal elder care services are scarce?

options.A: Families bear total, round-the-clock responsibility without institutional support systems
options.B: Local healthcare workers refuse to provide education on chronic illnesses
options.C: Traditional herbal remedies cure dementia symptoms and reduce care needs
options.D: Nigerian patients with dementia reject all forms of family involvement

explanation: The lack of structured day-care centers and formal respite facilities forces individual family members to shoulder the entire burden of care alone. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T10#GNS324_U4_T10_h7)

question: What defines a closed fracture?

options.A: The bone breaks into more than three pieces
options.B: The fracture heals without any medical intervention
options.C: The overlying skin remains intact over the break
options.D: The broken bone pierces through the skin

explanation: A closed fracture means the bone is broken internally, but the external skin barrier is uncompromised, which lowers infection risks. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h1)

question: Why are greenstick fractures frequently seen in young children?

options.A: Pediatric bones lack calcium and dense minerals
options.B: Children experience lower impact forces during falls
options.C: Children have more flexible and softer bones
options.D: Children heal much faster than adult patients

explanation: Children have immature, pliable bones that tend to bend and splinter rather than snap completely across. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h1)

question: The grating sound or feel produced by broken bone ends rubbing together is called what?

options.A: Ecchymosis
options.B: Crepitus
options.C: Edema
options.D: Clonus

explanation: Crepitus occurs when fractured bone fragments grind against each other, creating a distinct crunching sensation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h2)

question: A patient with a tibial fracture shows severe localized swelling and bruising. What causes this early bruising?

options.A: Bleeding into the soft tissues from ruptured blood vessels
options.B: Infection setting into the subcutaneous fat layers
options.C: Permanent destruction of superficial nerve endings
options.D: Reaction of the skin to tight plaster casting materials

explanation: Ecchymosis or bruising appears when blood escapes from damaged local blood vessels into the surrounding subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h2)

question: Which finding represents a late sign of neurovascular compromise in a fractured limb?

options.A: Increased capillary refill time
options.B: Absence of distal pulses
options.C: Mild swelling around the joint
options.D: Localized warmth over the skin

explanation: Disappearance of distal pulses indicates severe arterial obstruction and represents an advanced, critical stage of compromised blood flow. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h3)

question: A patient with a forearm cast complains of intense pain that does not respond to strong pain medication. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Normal healing process of the radius bone
options.B: Beginning stages of compartment syndrome
options.C: Allergic reaction to the synthetic plaster
options.D: Inadequate dietary calcium intake

explanation: Pain out of proportion to the injury that resists analgesia is the hallmark early warning sign of rising pressure inside a muscle compartment. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying traction to a fractured limb before surgery?

options.A: To permanently fuse the broken bone ends together
options.B: To administer intravenous antibiotics directly to bone
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for future surgery
options.D: To reduce muscle spasms and maintain bone alignment

explanation: Traction exerts a steady pulling force that overcomes natural muscle spasms and keeps bone ends aligned prior to definitive surgical repair. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why would an orthopedic surgeon choose an external fixator over internal plates for a severe open fracture?

options.A: External fixators allow easy access for wound care and manage damaged soft tissue
options.B: External fixators are permanently left inside the body without removal
options.C: External fixators completely prevent the occurrence of fat embolism syndrome
options.D: Internal plates increase the risk of rapid bone healing complications

explanation: When soft tissue is badly crushed or infected in an open fracture, external pins keep bones stable while leaving room to dress open wounds. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why must a fresh plaster cast be handled with the palms of the hands rather than the fingertips?

options.A: Palms generate heat that speeds up the drying process
options.B: Fingertips leave indentations that can cause pressure sores underneath
options.C: Finger pressure causes the wet cast to dissolve completely
options.D: Plaster material is extremely toxic to bare human skin

explanation: Depressions in a drying plaster cast create localized pressure points against the underlying skin, leading rapidly to tissue ischemia and ulceration. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h5)

question: A nurse enters a patient's room and notices the weights for skeletal traction are resting on the floor. What is the immediate action?

options.A: Leave the weights alone because traction tension is now optimal
options.B: Remove all the weights permanently to give the leg a rest
options.C: Ensure the weights hang freely without touching the floor or bed
options.D: Tighten the skin traction bandage around the lower calf area

explanation: Weights touching the floor lose their pulling force, rendering the traction completely ineffective at maintaining bone alignment and muscle relaxation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h5)

question: How much space should be maintained between the top of a properly fitted crutch and the patient's armpit?

options.A: One inch or half a finger width
options.B: Six full inches of clearance
options.C: Enough space to rest the entire shoulder
options.D: Two to three finger widths

explanation: Leaving two to three finger widths prevents crutch pressure from compressing the axillary blood vessels and nerves, which causes crutch paralysis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h6)

question: A patient with a fractured right leg is learning to walk up a flight of stairs using crutches. Which limb leads the movement upward?

options.A: The uninjured left leg
options.B: Both crutches simultaneously
options.C: The weaker side of the body
options.D: The fractured right leg

explanation: When going up stairs, the strong uninjured leg goes up first to lift the body weight, supported by the crutches, before the injured leg follows. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h6)

question: Which dietary nutrient is essential for the formation of the collagen matrix during bone healing?

options.A: Sodium
options.B: Trans fats
options.C: Protein
options.D: Simple sugars

explanation: Protein provides the fundamental amino building blocks required to synthesize collagen and build new bone matrix tissue. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h7)

question: Why is increased fluid and fiber intake particularly important for a patient confined to bed rest with a leg cast?

options.A: To speed up the drying time of plaster casts
options.B: To increase direct calcium absorption in the gut
options.C: To reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis
options.D: To prevent the development of painful constipation

explanation: Immobility and narcotic pain medications slow down bowel motility, making adequate fluid and fiber intake vital to prevent constipation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h7)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of fat embolism syndrome following a long bone fracture?

options.A: Respiratory distress and petechiae on the chest
options.B: Yellow discoloration of the sclera and palms
options.C: Inability to speak or comprehend simple commands
options.D: Sudden high fever and severe localized itching

explanation: Fat emboli travel to the lungs causing breathing difficulty, and to skin capillaries causing a characteristic petechial rash on the upper body. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h8)

question: Which nursing intervention best prevents deep vein thrombosis in a patient with a lower limb fracture?

options.A: Restricting daily fluid intake to decrease blood volume
options.B: Massaging the calves vigorously every hour to break up clots
options.C: Encouraging regular leg exercises and early ambulation when prescribed
options.D: Elevating the bed knee break position to maximum height

explanation: Promoting muscle movement and blood circulation through exercise and walking helps prevent venous stasis and clot formation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T11#GNS324_U4_T11_h8)

question: What is the primary medical goal of performing a surgical amputation?

options.A: To permanently eliminate all physical activity
options.B: To remove diseased or non-viable tissue
options.C: To completely prevent any future infections
options.D: To accelerate natural bone regeneration

explanation: Amputation removes non-functional or dangerous tissue to preserve the patient's overall health and prevent spreading complications. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h1)

question: A diabetic patient with severe ischemic gangrene of the foot undergoes surgery. What underlying pathological process most likely caused this outcome?

options.A: A localized soft-tissue allergic reaction
options.B: Rapidly spreading bone malignancy
options.C: An acute traumatic crush injury
options.D: Chronic peripheral vascular disease

explanation: Poor circulation from diabetes leads to chronic ischemia and tissue death, making vascular disease a leading cause of lower limb amputations. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h1)

question: A transtibial amputation is commonly referred to by what description?

options.A: Wrist disarticulation
options.B: Above knee amputation
options.C: Ankle disarticulation
options.D: Below knee amputation

explanation: Transtibial refers to the surgical removal of the lower leg occurring below the knee joint. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h2)

question: Why do surgeons prefer to preserve the knee joint during a lower extremity amputation when possible?

options.A: It completely prevents phantom limb pain occurrences
options.B: It reduces energy expenditure during future walking
options.C: It ensures faster closure of skin flaps
options.D: It eliminates the need for any surgical dressings

explanation: Preserving natural joints like the knee helps maintain a more normal gait and requires less physical exertion when using a prosthesis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h2)

question: What is a major positioning error to avoid during the first few days after an amputation?

options.A: Turning the patient frequently from side to side
options.B: Encouraging early deep breathing exercises
options.C: Prolonged elevation of the residual limb on pillows
options.D: Keeping the bed in a flat horizontal position

explanation: Keeping the stump elevated for more than 24 hours can cause joint contractures, making future prosthetic fitting difficult. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h3)

question: A patient returns from surgery following a right transfemoral amputation. Which immediate postoperative assessment takes highest priority?

options.A: Measuring the exact circumference of the residual limb
options.B: Assessing the patient's ability to operate a wheelchair
options.C: Checking the surgical dressing for signs of active bleeding
options.D: Inquiring about future career goals and employment

explanation: Hemorrhage is an immediate, life-threatening postoperative complication that requires constant vigilance and prompt intervention. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h3)

question: How should a patient properly clean their residual limb during daily hygiene routines?

options.A: Apply medicated petroleum jelly and wrap tightly
options.B: Soak the limb in hot water for at least one hour
options.C: Wash with mild soap and warm water, then pat dry
options.D: Scrub vigorously with a stiff brush and antiseptic

explanation: Gentle cleansing prevents skin irritation, and thorough drying stops moisture accumulation that attracts bacterial or fungal infections. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h4)

question: Why is a figure-eight bandage wrapping technique used on a residual limb?

options.A: To completely cut off blood supply to the distal end
options.B: To anchor the skin tightly to the underlying bone
options.C: To stimulate rapid hair growth on the surgical site
options.D: To evenly distribute pressure and reduce post-surgical edema

explanation: Figure-eight wrapping prevents the tourniquet effect while effectively shrinking and shaping the limb for future prosthetic use. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h4)

question: What term describes the burning or shooting sensation a patient feels in a limb that has been removed?

options.A: Phantom limb pain
options.B: Neuromuscular contracture
options.C: Referred visceral pain
options.D: Incisional wound pain

explanation: Phantom limb pain is a neuropathic sensation where the brain continues to register sensory input from the missing body part. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h5)

question: Which drug class is commonly prescribed to manage neuropathic phantom limb pain?

options.A: Short-acting loop diuretics
options.B: Anticonvulsants like gabapentin
options.C: Broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
options.D: Topical skeletal muscle relaxants

explanation: Neuropathic pain responds well to medications that stabilize nerve signaling, such as gabapentin or certain antidepressants. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h5)

question: What position should a lower-extremity amputee assume daily to stretch hip flexors and prevent contractures?

options.A: Side-lying with knees pulled up
options.B: Semi-Fowler position in bed
options.C: Prone lying flat on the stomach
options.D: Sitting upright in a high armchair

explanation: Lying prone extends the hip joint, directly counteracting the flexion contractures commonly caused by sitting or propping the stump. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h6)

question: Why is early upper body strengthening especially important for a patient with a lower limb amputation?

options.A: To improve respiratory volume and prevent lung infections
options.B: To support the future use of assistive devices like crutches
options.C: To eliminate the possibility of phantom limb sensations
options.D: To accelerate the healing of the surgical skin incision

explanation: Upper body strength is essential for managing walkers, crutches, and wheelchair propulsion during early rehabilitation phases. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention best helps a patient cope with a altered body image after an amputation?

options.A: Encouraging the patient to avoid looking at the stump
options.B: Providing a safe space to express feelings and fears
options.C: Insisting that the patient remain in bed to rest
options.D: Minimizing discussion about the missing limb entirely

explanation: Open communication and emotional validation help patients process grief and adapt to changes in their body image. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary benefit of introducing a peer support visitor who also has an amputation?

options.A: It offers practical insight and hope for future rehabilitation
options.B: It speeds up the surgical wound healing process
options.C: It replaces the need for formal physical therapy sessions
options.D: It guarantees complete elimination of phantom limb pain

explanation: Seeing someone successfully navigate life after an amputation provides realistic encouragement and reduces feelings of isolation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h7)

question: Which home modification is most important to prevent accidental falls for a recovering amputee?

options.A: Installing heavy blackout curtains in bedrooms
options.B: Painting the walls in bright contrasting colors
options.C: Replacing all wooden furniture with soft cushions
options.D: Removing loose throw rugs and hallway clutter

explanation: Clear walkways prevent tripping hazards for patients learning to use assistive mobility devices or prosthetics. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h8)

question: Which finding on a residual limb requires immediate reporting to the healthcare provider?

options.A: Foul-smelling drainage and spreading redness around the incision
options.B: Temporary tingling felt in the missing toes during rest
options.C: Slight skin dryness that improves with mild soap washing
options.D: Mild itching sensation reported around the healing suture line

explanation: Foul discharge and spreading erythema are classic signs of surgical site infection that require medical evaluation and treatment. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h8)

question: What term describes vision loss that cannot be corrected by standard eyeglasses?

options.A: Presbyopia
options.B: Low vision
options.C: Astigmatism
options.D: Strabismus

explanation: Low vision refers to visual impairment that standard lenses or surgery cannot completely fix, leaving some functional sight. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h1)

question: Total blindness is best identified by which clinical finding?

options.A: Blurry vision correctable by surgery
options.B: Tunnel vision with clear central fields
options.C: Complete absence of light perception
options.D: Inability to read newspaper print

explanation: Total blindness means the eye cannot perceive any light or form at all. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h1)

question: The leading cause of reversible blindness worldwide is what eye condition?

options.A: Glaucoma
options.B: Macular degeneration
options.C: Cataracts
options.D: Trachoma

explanation: Cataracts involve clouding of the lens and can be successfully treated with surgical removal. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h2)

question: Increased intraocular pressure is the primary pathological feature of which eye disease?

options.A: Retinopathy
options.B: Cataracts
options.C: Conjunctivitis
options.D: Glaucoma

explanation: Glaucoma builds pressure inside the eyeball, slowly destroying the optic nerve fibers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h2)

question: The standard tool used for testing central distance visual acuity in clinical settings is what chart?

options.A: Jaeger card
options.B: Snellen chart
options.C: Ishihara chart
options.D: Amsler grid

explanation: The Snellen chart is the classic tool featuring rows of letters used to measure distance vision. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h3)

question: A patient with suspected peripheral vision loss from glaucoma should be evaluated using which method?

options.A: Ophthalmoscope examination
options.B: Confrontation test
options.C: Color blindness plates
options.D: Direct pupillary light reflex

explanation: The confrontation test is a quick bedside method to check for gross defects in the patient's visual fields. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h3)

question: Why is establishing consistent spatial routines important for patients with severe visual impairment?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any assistive mobility devices
options.B: It restores lost visual acuity in the peripheral fields
options.C: It cures the underlying degenerative eye disease over time
options.D: It prevents accidental falls by maintaining predictable pathways

explanation: Keeping furniture and personal items in exact, unchanging places helps patients navigate safely without bumping into obstacles. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h4)

question: The first action a nurse should take when entering the home of a blind patient is what?

options.A: Verbally announce their presence and identity
options.B: Rearrange the furniture to create a safe walking path
options.C: Immediately touch the patient's shoulder to reassure them
options.D: Check all medication bottles for expiration dates

explanation: Speaking first prevents startling a visually impaired person who cannot see someone approach. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h4)

question: What simple home modification helps prevent slips in the bathroom for visually impaired patients?

options.A: Placing non-slip mats inside the bathtub
options.B: Installing bright flashing emergency lights
options.C: Removing all doors to improve ventilation
options.D: Covering windows with heavy dark curtains

explanation: Non-slip rubber mats provide vital friction to prevent dangerous falls in wet bathroom areas. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h5)

question: Painting stair edges with a contrasting bright color serves what main safety purpose?

options.A: It signals family members when the stairs need cleaning
options.B: It strengthens the structural stability of the steps
options.C: It disinfects the wooden surface against bacterial growth
options.D: It helps patients with partial vision judge step boundaries clearly

explanation: High-contrast markers make transitions between different step levels visible to those with low vision. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h5)

question: The traditional tool used by visually impaired individuals for independent outdoor mobility is which item?

options.A: Magnifying glass
options.B: Acoustic headset
options.C: Guide wheelchair
options.D: White cane

explanation: The white cane is a universal mobility tool that helps users detect ground obstacles and alerts others to their visual impairment. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary role of an Orientation and Mobility specialist in patient care?

options.A: Performing surgical operations for cataracts and glaucoma
options.B: Prescribing corrective laser eye surgery procedures
options.C: Managing pharmacological treatments for retinal disorders
options.D: Teaching safe navigation and environmental mapping skills

explanation: These specialists train patients to travel independently and safely both indoors and outdoors. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h6)

question: A patient newly diagnosed with permanent blindness is most likely experiencing which psychological response?

options.A: A grief reaction similar to mourning a major loss
options.B: Aggressive hostility directed exclusively at the nursing staff
options.C: Complete indifference toward their medical prognosis
options.D: Immediate and effortless acceptance of their new lifestyle

explanation: Losing sight represents a major life alteration that typically triggers emotional stages of grief and adjustment. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h7)

question: How can family members best support a visually impaired relative without hindering recovery?

options.A: Limiting social visitors to protect them from emotional stress
options.B: Insisting the patient stay indoors to avoid potential public accidents
options.C: Encouraging independence while offering help only when requested
options.D: Taking over all daily self-care tasks to eliminate any mistakes

explanation: Balanced support fosters self-reliance and prevents the negative psychological effects of overprotection. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T13#GNS324_U4_T13_h7)

question: What is the main difference between being deaf and being hard of hearing?

options.A: Presence of chronic middle ear infections
options.B: Inability to produce vocal sounds
options.C: Inability to process linguistic information through sound
options.D: Total absence of auditory nerve structures

explanation: Deafness means hearing loss is severe enough that a person cannot successfully process speech and language using sound alone, even when wearing hearing aids. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h1)

question: Which communication method does a patient with profound hearing loss rely on the most?

options.A: Amplified telephone devices
options.B: Visual cues and sign language
options.C: High-frequency audio tones
options.D: Bone conduction headsets

explanation: Profound hearing loss makes hearing unreliable, so patients shift toward visual communication channels like sign language and gestures. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h1)

question: What are the names of the three tiny bones in the middle ear?

options.A: Pinna, tragus, and lobule
options.B: Semicircular canals and ampulla
options.C: Cochlea, vestibule, and utricle
options.D: Malleus, incus, and stapes

explanation: The malleus, incus, and stapes link together to form a chain that carries sound vibrations across the middle ear. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h2)

question: Which part of the inner ear turns fluid vibrations into nerve impulses?

options.A: The cochlea
options.B: The tympanic membrane
options.C: The Eustachian tube
options.D: The external auditory meatus

explanation: The cochlea contains tiny hair cells that move when fluid waves pass through, creating electrical signals for the brain. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h2)

question: What is the primary cause of conductive hearing loss?

options.A: Impeded sound transmission through the outer or middle ear
options.B: Permanent damage to the auditory cortex in the brain
options.C: Degeneration of hair cells within the cochlea
options.D: Complete destruction of the vestibulocochlear nerve

explanation: Conductive hearing loss happens when something blocks sound waves from traveling properly through the outer ear canal or middle ear. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h3)

question: An elderly patient experiencing presbycusis typically has which type of hearing loss?

options.A: Conductive hearing loss
options.B: Sensorineural hearing loss
options.C: Central auditory processing disorder
options.D: Functional hearing loss

explanation: Age-related hearing loss, or presbycusis, is caused by the gradual breakdown of sensory hair cells inside the inner ear cochlea. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h3)

question: Which group of medications is well known for causing ototoxicity and hearing damage?

options.A: Inhaled corticosteroids
options.B: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
options.C: Loop diuretics for hypertension
options.D: Aminoglycoside antibiotics

explanation: Certain antibiotics, such as gentamicin, can harm inner ear structures if drug levels in the blood are not monitored. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h4)

question: Which infection during pregnancy often leads to congenital deafness in the newborn?

options.A: Rubella
options.B: Malaria
options.C: Typhoid fever
options.D: Tetanus

explanation: Maternal rubella infection, especially in the first trimester, can disrupt the normal development of the baby's ears. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h4)

question: During a Weber tuning fork test, sound is heard louder in the impaired ear. What does this indicate?

options.A: Conductive hearing loss in that ear
options.B: Sensorineural hearing loss in that ear
options.C: Normal hearing bilaterally
options.D: Complete bilateral deafness

explanation: With a conductive loss, outside room noise is blocked out, making bone-conducted sound seem louder in the affected ear. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h5)

question: What is the main goal of pure-tone audiometry testing?

options.A: Visualizing the physical integrity of the tympanic membrane
options.B: Assessing the vestibular balance system in the inner ear
options.C: Measuring exact hearing thresholds across different sound frequencies
options.D: Detecting active bacterial infections in the ear canal

explanation: Pure-tone audiometry measures the softest sounds a patient can hear at different pitches and plots them on a chart. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h5)

question: What is the best way to start a conversation with a hospitalized deaf patient?

options.A: Begin talking immediately while completing charting tasks
options.B: Speak quickly so the patient can read lips faster
options.C: Gently wave or turn on a light to gain visual attention
options.D: Stand behind the bed and speak in a very loud voice

explanation: Deaf patients depend on sight. Getting their visual attention first prevents startling them and helps them focus on you. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h6)

question: Which action should nurses avoid when talking to a patient who reads lips?

options.A: Minimizing background noise in the room
options.B: Ensuring good lighting on the speaker's face
options.C: Standing directly in front of the patient
options.D: Exaggerating mouth movements and shouting

explanation: Shouting and over-exaggerating words distorts natural facial expressions and lip shapes, making lip-reading much harder. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h6)

question: How does a cochlear implant work differently from a regular hearing aid?

options.A: It simply makes all ambient sounds louder within the ear canal
options.B: It uses bone conduction behind the ear to transmit vibrations
options.C: It bypasses damaged hair cells to directly stimulate the auditory nerve
options.D: It surgically removes obstructions from the middle ear cavity

explanation: Cochlear implants change sound waves into electrical signals that stimulate the auditory nerve directly, helping people with severe inner ear damage. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h7)

question: Which home modification is most helpful for keeping a deaf person safe?

options.A: Brightly colored wall decorations
options.B: High-decibel audible alarm systems
options.C: Flashing strobe light smoke detectors
options.D: Standard telephone ring amplifiers

explanation: Visual alerts like flashing strobe lights make sure that individuals with profound hearing loss are instantly warned during emergencies. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T14#GNS324_U4_T14_h7)

question: What is the main problem inside cells that leads to cancer?

options.A: Cells divide out of control due to gene changes
options.B: Cells stop all metabolic activity completely
options.C: Cells multiply normally only in local areas
options.D: Cells undergo rapid programmed death everywhere

explanation: Cancer starts when damaged genes fail to control the cell cycle, causing cells to multiply without stopping. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h1)

question: How do malignant tumors mainly differ from benign tumors?

options.A: Malignant tumors can invade tissues and spread to other parts
options.B: Malignant tumors are always safely enclosed in local tissues
options.C: Benign tumors grow much faster than malignant ones
options.D: Benign tumors frequently spread to distant organs

explanation: Malignant cells break away from the main tumor and travel through the blood or lymph to form new growths elsewhere. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h1)

question: Which type of cancer starts in the tissues that line body surfaces and organs?

options.A: Myelomas
options.B: Sarcomas
options.C: Carcinomas
options.D: Leukemias

explanation: Carcinomas are the most common type of cancer, growing in the epithelial cells found in skin, glands, and organ linings. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h2)

question: A tumor found in a patient's thigh muscle belongs to which cancer category?

options.A: Carcinoma
options.B: Sarcoma
options.C: Lymphoma
options.D: Leukemia

explanation: Muscles, bones, and fat are connective tissues, and cancers that start in these tissues are called sarcomas. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h2)

question: A long-lasting infection with the Human Papillomavirus is a major risk factor for which cancer?

options.A: Lung cancer
options.B: Liver cancer
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Stomach cancer

explanation: High-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus are directly linked to cell changes in the cervix that can turn into cancer. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h3)

question: Which viral infection is strongly linked to liver cancer cases in Nigeria?

options.A: Cytomegalovirus
options.B: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.C: Epstein-Barr Virus
options.D: Hepatitis B

explanation: Long-term infection with Hepatitis B or C causes ongoing liver damage and scarring, which greatly raises the risk of liver cancer. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h3)

question: What is a common whole-body sign often seen in people with cancer?

options.A: Sudden weight gain
options.B: Higher red blood cell count
options.C: Unexplained weight loss
options.D: Increased muscle strength

explanation: Cancer changes how the body uses energy, often leading to rapid weight loss and body wasting. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h4)

question: Which symptom is a typical early warning sign of a local tumor?

options.A: Skin rash from a new soap
options.B: A hard, painless lump in the breast
options.C: Body aches after hard exercise
options.D: Sneezing from seasonal allergies

explanation: New, hard, and painless lumps growing inside tissues are often the first physical clue of a localized tumor. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h4)

question: Which test gives the only sure confirmation that a patient has cancer?

options.A: Routine blood count
options.B: Tissue biopsy
options.C: Ultrasound scan
options.D: Physical exam

explanation: A pathologist must look at a sample of the tissue under a microscope to confirm the presence of cancer cells. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h5)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Mutation
options.B: Morphology
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Malignancy

explanation: The TNM system looks at the primary Tumor size, nearby lymph Node involvement, and distant Metastasis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h5)

question: How does chemotherapy mainly work in the body?

options.A: By destroying cells that divide rapidly
options.B: By coating healthy tissues to block bacteria
options.C: By increasing red blood cell production
options.D: By repairing damaged DNA inside normal cells

explanation: Chemotherapy drugs target fast-dividing cells, which includes cancer cells as well as normal cells like hair roots. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is the main goal of surgery for early-stage cancer?

options.A: To replace damaged organs with donor organs
options.B: To deliver radiation directly into the bloodstream
options.C: To remove the local tumor completely with clear edges
options.D: To boost the immune system against widespread disease

explanation: Surgery is used to cut out the main tumor mass before it has a chance to spread to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is a key way to prevent infections for a patient having chemotherapy at home?

options.A: Wash hands often and stay away from crowded places
options.B: Limit drinking water to avoid bathroom trips
options.C: Eat raw, unwashed vegetables for extra vitamins
options.D: Stop all physical activity to save energy

explanation: Chemotherapy lowers white blood cell counts, leaving patients vulnerable to infections. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h7)

question: A family caregiver calls to say their relative on cancer treatment has a new fever. What should the nurse advise?

options.A: Wait a full day to see if the temperature drops
options.B: Encourage heavy exercise to sweat out the fever
options.C: Call the cancer treatment team right away
options.D: Give a sleeping pill to help the patient rest

explanation: A fever in a patient with a weak immune system is an emergency that needs quick medical check and antibiotics. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h7)

question: What is the main goal of palliative care in cancer treatment?

options.A: To make life longer no matter how uncomfortable it is
options.B: To fix the gene changes that caused the disease
options.C: To improve quality of life and relieve tough symptoms
options.D: To get rid of the tumor completely from the body

explanation: Palliative care focuses on comfort, pain relief, and emotional support for patients and families facing serious illness. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h8)

question: When can palliative care services start during a cancer illness?

options.A: After all cancer drugs have failed
options.B: At any stage, alongside regular medical treatments
options.C: Before any tests or staging are done
options.D: Only during the very last days of life

explanation: Palliative care is not just for end-of-life care; it can start early to help manage symptoms while treatment is ongoing. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T15#GNS324_U4_T15_h8)

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Systolic pressure
options.B: Venous pressure
options.C: Diastolic pressure
options.D: Pulse pressure

explanation: The top number measures the force exerted on arterial walls when the heart contracts. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h1)

question: Why is high blood pressure often called a silent killer?

options.A: It only affects people during sleep
options.B: Patients usually show no obvious early symptoms
options.C: Blood pressure cuffs fail to detect high readings
options.D: The condition resolves without medical intervention

explanation: High blood pressure often develops without any noticeable signs, meaning people can have it for years without knowing until damage occurs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h1)

question: A blood pressure reading of 142/92 mmHg falls into which category?

options.A: Prehypertension
options.B: Normal blood pressure
options.C: Stage 1 Hypertension
options.D: Stage 2 Hypertension

explanation: A systolic reading between 140 and 159 combined with a diastolic reading between 90 and 99 is classified as Stage 1 hypertension. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h2)

question: What are the two main factors that determine a person's blood pressure?

options.A: Cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance
options.B: Blood volume and hemoglobin concentration
options.C: Heart rate and respiratory rate
options.D: Sodium intake and potassium excretion

explanation: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps out and the resistance the blood meets as it flows through the vessels. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h2)

question: What type describes the majority of high blood pressure cases seen in the clinic?

options.A: Gestational hypertension
options.B: Primary hypertension
options.C: Secondary hypertension
options.D: Resistant hypertension

explanation: Primary or essential hypertension is the most common form, meaning it develops over time without a single identifiable medical cause. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h3)

question: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops high blood pressure. What type of hypertension is this?

options.A: Primary hypertension
options.B: Idiopathic hypertension
options.C: Essential hypertension
options.D: Secondary hypertension

explanation: When high blood pressure stems from a known identifiable medical condition like kidney disease, it is classified as secondary. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h3)

question: How long should a patient rest before you take their blood pressure?

options.A: Thirty seconds
options.B: Fifteen minutes
options.C: Five minutes
options.D: One hour

explanation: Resting quietly for five minutes allows the patient's body to settle, ensuring an accurate baseline measurement. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h4)

question: A home care nurse notices a blood pressure cuff bladder covers only half of the client's large upper arm. What is the most likely effect on the reading?

options.A: The reading will be falsely elevated
options.B: The device will fail to record any numbers
options.C: The reading will remain completely accurate
options.D: The reading will be falsely lowered

explanation: Using an undersized cuff requires excessive pressure to compress the large arm tissue, producing a falsely high blood pressure reading. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h4)

question: Why do many patients with high blood pressure stop taking their daily medication?

options.A: Blood pressure always remains low permanently after one dose
options.B: They feel fine and assume the condition is cured
options.C: Antihypertensive drugs cause instant memory loss
options.D: Pharmacies never run out of stock

explanation: Because high blood pressure usually has no symptoms, patients often feel completely healthy and mistakenly think they no longer need treatment. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h5)

question: What common side effect should a nurse warn a client about when starting a new antihypertensive medication?

options.A: Orthostatic hypotension
options.B: Uncontrolled weight gain
options.C: Sudden permanent blindness
options.D: Severe muscle enlargement

explanation: Blood pressure medications can cause sudden drops in pressure when changing positions, leading to dizziness. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h5)

question: What dietary pattern is specifically recommended to help lower blood pressure naturally?

options.A: High protein ketogenic diet
options.B: High sodium traditional diet
options.C: Low fiber liquid diet
options.D: DASH diet

explanation: The DASH diet focuses on fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy while restricting sodium to manage blood pressure. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h6)

question: How does regular exercise help manage high blood pressure over time?

options.A: It strengthens the cardiovascular system and improves vessel health
options.B: It increases total body fat storage rapidly
options.C: It raises resting heart rate to maximum levels
options.D: It eliminates the need for any future medical checkups

explanation: Consistent physical activity makes the heart a more efficient pump and keeps blood vessels flexible. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h6)

question: What blood pressure measurement is considered a hypertensive crisis?

options.A: Exceeding 120/80 mmHg
options.B: Exceeding 180/120 mmHg
options.C: Exceeding 160/100 mmHg
options.D: Exceeding 140/90 mmHg

explanation: Readings above 180/120 mmHg signal a dangerous spike that requires immediate medical attention. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h7)

question: What is the primary difference between hypertensive urgency and hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Response to oral hydration alone
options.B: The time of day the symptoms start
options.C: Presence of acute target organ damage
options.D: Age of the affected individual

explanation: An emergency involves active damage to organs like the brain or kidneys, whereas urgency does not show immediate organ injury. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h7)

question: Which organ is strained when long-term high blood pressure causes left ventricular hypertrophy?

options.A: The liver
options.B: The lungs
options.C: The stomach
options.D: The heart

explanation: Constant high pressure forces the heart's main pumping chamber to work harder, causing the muscle wall to thicken. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h8)

question: Why is it important for community nurses to ask patients about local herbal remedies?

options.A: Herbal remedies permanently cure essential hypertension
options.B: Hospitals require patients to bring herbs for admission
options.C: Some local herbs can interact negatively with prescribed blood pressure drugs
options.D: Traditional leaves are the only approved medical treatment

explanation: Unregulated herbal mixtures can interfere with hospital medications, either making them too strong or blocking their effects. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h8)

question: Which cells in the pancreas are responsible for producing insulin?

options.A: Alpha cells
options.B: Beta cells
options.C: Delta cells
options.D: Acinar cells
