explanation: Insulin is synthesized and secreted by the beta cells located within the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h1)

question: What happens in the body when there is not enough insulin or when insulin doesn't work properly?

options.A: Red blood cells destroy circulating nutrients
options.B: The pancreas stops producing digestive enzymes
options.C: Cells rapidly absorb too much sugar
options.D: Glucose accumulates in the bloodstream

explanation: Without enough working insulin, sugar can't get inside your body's cells for energy, so it builds up in your blood (hyperglycemia). You've got this! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h1)

question: What is the main underlying cause of Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Gradual resistance of muscle cells to insulin
options.B: Severe dietary deficiency of essential vitamins
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.D: Temporary hormonal changes during pregnancy

explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas. Keep up the great study habit! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h2)

question: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Type 2 requires immediate lifelong oral medication without dietary changes
options.B: Type 2 is strictly an acute condition that resolves without long-term treatment
options.C: Type 2 only affects elderly patients who have a family history of kidney disease
options.D: Type 2 involves insulin resistance and relative deficiency rather than total destruction

explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, your body still makes insulin, but your cells resist using it properly—unlike Type 1 where the beta cells are completely wiped out. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the excessive thirst that a diabetic patient often feels?

options.A: Polyphagia
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polydipsia
options.D: Paresthesia

explanation: Polydipsia simply means extreme thirst. It happens because the body is losing a lot of water through frequent urination (polyuria). You are building a solid clinical vocabulary! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h3)

question: Why do patients with untreated diabetes sometimes experience rapid weight loss?

options.A: Excessive fluid intake flushes away all dietary nutrients
options.B: High blood sugar levels speed up the normal metabolic rate
options.C: Kidneys filter out solid food particles into the urine
options.D: The body breaks down stored fat and muscle for energy

explanation: When glucose can't enter the cells for fuel, the body panics and starts burning its own fat and muscle instead, causing sudden weight loss. Makes total sense when you picture it! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h3)

question: Which medication is absolutely essential for a patient living with Type 1 diabetes to survive?

options.A: Metformin
options.B: Acarbose
options.C: Sulfonylurea
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Because Type 1 bodies cannot make insulin, daily insulin replacement is a matter of survival. Another win for your clinical knowledge today! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h4)

question: A patient with rapid-acting insulin asks when they should take their injection. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Only right before going to sleep at night
options.B: Just before or right at mealtime
options.C: Two hours after finishing the meal
options.D: Once a week on an empty stomach

explanation: Rapid-acting insulin starts working very quickly, so patients take it right as they eat to match the incoming food sugars. Spot on! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h4)

question: Which type of food has the most direct and immediate effect on blood sugar levels?

options.A: Pure water
options.B: Carbohydrates
options.C: Dietary minerals
options.D: Healthy fats

explanation: Carbs break down into glucose during digestion, making them the number one food group to watch for blood sugar management. You're cruising through these! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h5)

question: Why do dietitians recommend high-fiber complex carbs instead of simple sugars for diabetic patients?

options.A: They stimulate the pancreas to grow new beta cells
options.B: They contain zero calories and cannot be converted into fat
options.C: They slow down digestion and prevent rapid blood sugar spikes
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for any diabetes medication

explanation: High-fiber carbs take longer to digest, giving a nice, steady release of energy rather than sending blood sugar through the roof. Brilliant nursing logic! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h5)

question: How does regular physical exercise help lower a person's blood sugar?

options.A: By permanently curing pancreatic beta cell damage
options.B: By destroying excess sugar in the bloodstream
options.C: By increasing insulin sensitivity in muscle cells
options.D: By slowing down overall body metabolism

explanation: Exercise tunes up your muscle cells so they respond better to insulin, helping them pull glucose out of the blood much easier. Keep up the momentum! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h6)

question: Why is daily foot care and inspection so crucial for patients with diabetes?

options.A: Daily observation increases blood circulation to the toes
options.B: Sweat buildup guarantees the rapid development of gangrene
options.C: Nerve damage can prevent them from feeling minor cuts or blisters
options.D: Skin color changes indicate the exact blood sugar level

explanation: Diabetes can cause nerve damage (neuropathy) in the feet, meaning minor sores can go unnoticed and turn into major wounds if not checked daily. Essential nursing wisdom! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h6)

question: Which of these is a classic example of a microvascular (small blood vessel) complication of diabetes?

options.A: Diabetic retinopathy affecting the eyes
options.B: Peripheral vascular disease in the legs
options.C: Coronary artery disease leading to angina
options.D: Cerebrospinal stroke affecting speech

explanation: Retinopathy damages the tiny, delicate blood vessels in the eyes, which makes it a classic microvascular complication. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h7)

question: What is the primary trigger for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.A: Consuming too much dietary protein in a single sitting
options.B: An allergic reaction to oral anti-diabetic medications
options.C: Severe lack of insulin forcing the body to break down fat rapidly
options.D: Sudden extreme physical exhaustion after heavy exercise

explanation: When insulin is severely lacking, the body burns fat too fast for fuel. This creates acidic waste products called ketones, leading to DKA. You're mastering advanced concepts! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h7)

question: What is the ultimate goal of patient education when teaching someone how to care for their diabetes at home?

options.A: Preventing the patient from ever experiencing normal life stress
options.B: Eliminating all future visits to the primary healthcare clinic
options.C: Empowering the patient to safely manage their daily condition
options.D: Ensuring the family takes complete control of medication administration

explanation: Good education gives patients the tools, knowledge, and confidence to take charge of their own health every day. Love to see it! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h8)

question: Which teaching style works best when you are educating a patient who was just diagnosed with diabetes?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on severe complications like kidney failure
options.B: Tailoring information to fit the patient's daily routine and lifestyle
options.C: Insisting that they completely change their diet in one single day
options.D: Handing them a complex medical textbook to read overnight

explanation: Teaching works best when it's practical, personalized, and fits smoothly into the patient's real everyday life. Fantastic work finishing this set! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h8)

question: Which germ is the main cause of tuberculosis (TB)?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
options.D: Bordetella pertussis

explanation: TB is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It loves to settle in the lungs! You'll get this easily with practice. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h1)

question: How does tuberculosis mostly spread from one person to another?

options.A: Ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products
options.B: Direct contact with contaminated skin lesions
options.C: Inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: Sharing eating utensils and drinking cups

explanation: When someone with active TB coughs or sneezes, tiny droplets float into the air. If others breathe them in, they can catch the infection too. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h1)

question: What is the key feature of a latent tuberculosis infection?

options.A: The patient has a productive cough and bloody sputum
options.B: The person is asymptomatic and cannot spread the disease
options.C: The bacteria are rapidly multiplying throughout the bloodstream
options.D: Chest X-rays consistently show severe lung cavity destruction

explanation: Latent TB means the germs are sleeping safely inside the body, kept in check by your immune system. The person feels fine and cannot pass it to others. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h2)

question: Why does the body form small bumps called granulomas during a TB infection?

options.A: To help transport oxygen across damaged alveolar membranes
options.B: To produce antibodies that neutralize the bacterial toxins
options.C: To wall off and contain the bacteria within the lungs
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of red blood cells

explanation: Think of granulomas as a smart defensive wall built by your immune system to trap the TB germs so they cannot wander around your lungs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h2)

question: Which breathing sign is a classic warning of active pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: A persistent cough lasting longer than three weeks
options.B: Sudden wheezing and severe shortness of breath
options.C: A sharp, barking cough triggered by cold air
options.D: Copious amounts of clear, watery nasal discharge

explanation: Any cough hanging around for more than three weeks should immediately make you think of TB and prompt a check-up! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h3)

question: A patient with active tuberculosis usually reports which set of body-wide signs?

options.A: Sudden weight gain, severe headache, and lethargy
options.B: Night sweats, low-grade fevers, and weight loss
options.C: Constipation, blurred vision, and muscle spasms
options.D: High fever, severe joint swelling, and a skin rash

explanation: Active TB drains the body's energy. Classic signs include drenching night sweats, afternoon fevers, and losing weight without trying. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h3)

question: What is the main drawback of a positive Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test?

options.A: It cannot distinguish between latent and active infection
options.B: It only works in patients who have never received vaccinations
options.C: It is completely unreliable for diagnosing immunocompromised adults
options.D: It requires laboratory analysis of blood within two hours

explanation: A positive skin test simply means your immune system has seen TB before. It cannot tell if the infection is sleeping (latent) or active. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h4)

question: Which test gives the final confirmation that a patient has active lung TB?

options.A: Physical auscultation of bilateral lung sounds
options.B: Routine complete blood count and electrolyte panel
options.C: Measurement of resting blood pressure and pulse rate
options.D: Sputum culture and acid-fast bacilli smear testing

explanation: Checking the patient's sputum for acid-fast bacilli or growing the germs in a lab gives the definitive proof needed to confirm active TB. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h4)

question: What is the main goal of Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) for TB patients?

options.A: Reducing the overall financial cost of purchasing prescription drugs
options.B: Eliminating the need for periodic sputum laboratory testing
options.C: Ensuring patients swallow every medication dose to prevent resistance
options.D: Allowing nurses to monitor daily lung function and oxygen saturation

explanation: With DOT, a health worker watches the patient take their drugs. This stops missed doses and prevents drug-resistant TB strains from forming. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h5)

question: Why do doctors treat active tuberculosis with several drugs at once instead of just one?

options.A: To counteract the severe sedative side effects of rifampin
options.B: To prevent the bacteria from developing drug resistance
options.C: To speed up the healing process so drugs are only taken for days
options.D: To completely eliminate normal flora in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: Hitting TB bacteria with multiple drugs makes it super hard for them to mutate and survive. Multi-drug therapy is a lifesaver! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h5)

question: What type of mask must nurses wear when walking into an active TB patient's room?

options.A: Standard paper surgical mask for fluid splashes
options.B: Particulate respirator such as an N95 mask
options.C: Cloth face covering made from thick cotton fabric
options.D: Plastic face shield with no respiratory filter

explanation: Because TB travels on tiny air particles, ordinary surgical masks won't cut it. An N95 respirator keeps healthcare workers safe! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h6)

question: Which simple home practice helps cut down the spread of airborne TB?

options.A: Keeping the patient bedroom door tightly locked at all times
options.B: Using chemical disinfectants to wipe down furniture daily
options.C: Washing all patient eating utensils in boiling water
options.D: Opening windows frequently to ensure good room ventilation

explanation: Fresh air is a powerful ally! Opening windows blows away and dilutes airborne TB germs so others don't breathe them in. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h6)

question: Which vitamin is often given alongside isoniazid to protect a patient's nerves?

options.A: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3)
options.B: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
options.C: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C)
options.D: Tocopherol (Vitamin E)

explanation: Isoniazid can drain Vitamin B6 levels, leading to tingling or nerve pain. Adding Vitamin B6 prevents this pesky side effect. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h7)

question: Why must patients finish their full course of TB drugs even after they start feeling better?

options.A: The body needs time to rebuild depleted stomach lining cells
options.B: Health authorities require written proof of finishing all pills
options.C: Stopping early causes immediate permanent liver failure
options.D: Remaining bacteria can multiply and cause drug-resistant relapse

explanation: Feeling better doesn't mean all germs are gone. The toughest ones are still hiding and will bounce back stronger if treatment stops early. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h7)

question: What is a normal and harmless effect of rifampin that nurses should warn patients about?

options.A: Bright green coloration of saliva and fingernails
options.B: Permanent yellow tinting of the skin and eye sclera
options.C: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears
options.D: Severe darkening of the skin on the hands and feet

explanation: Rifampin naturally dyes body fluids a reddish-orange color. It looks alarming, but it's completely normal and harmless! [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h8)

question: Which anti-TB drug requires regular checks on a patient's vision and color sight?

options.A: Pyrazinamide
options.B: Isoniazid
options.C: Rifampin
options.D: Ethambutol

explanation: Ethambutol can affect eye health (optic neuritis). Regular eye checks help catch any vision changes early before they become serious. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T18#GNS324_U4_T18_h8)

question: How would you best describe depression in a clinical setting?

options.A: A temporary lack of vitamins causing physical weakness
options.B: A minor behavioral adjustment issue in older adults
options.C: A serious mood disorder affecting thoughts and daily activities
options.D: A temporary emotional reaction to physical fatigue

explanation: Spot on! Depression isn't just a brief bad mood or fatigue; it's a true mood disorder that impacts a person's entire daily life and well-being. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is it important for nurses to look beyond purely physical complaints when checking for depression?

options.A: Patients will always directly report feeling sad without prompting
options.B: Physical complaints always disappear once mental health improves
options.C: Depression frequently presents itself disguised as chronic pain or fatigue
options.D: Physical symptoms are completely unrelated to psychological health

explanation: Great job! Patients often show up with body aches, headaches, or extreme tiredness rather than saying they feel sad. Staying alert to this helps us catch what's really going on. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h1)

question: Which type of depression tends to happen during specific times of the year, especially the cold winter months?

options.A: Seasonal affective disorder
options.B: Postpartum depression
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Persistent depressive disorder

explanation: You got it! Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) kicks in during certain seasons, usually when daylight gets shorter in the winter. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h2)

question: How is persistent depressive disorder different from major depressive disorder?

options.A: It affects only new mothers following childbirth
options.B: It only occurs during the winter months of the year
options.C: It is a chronic, milder form lasting for two years or longer
options.D: It lasts for exactly two weeks before disappearing entirely

explanation: Spot on! Persistent depressive disorder hangs around for a long time—two years or more—even if the daily symptoms are a bit milder than major depression. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which chemical messengers in the brain play a major role in mood and depression?

options.A: Serotonin and norepinephrine
options.B: Insulin and glucagon
options.C: Thyroxine and calcitonin
options.D: Sodium and potassium

explanation: Well done! Serotonin and norepinephrine are key neurotransmitters that help regulate our mood. An imbalance here is a big part of why depression happens. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h3)

question: A patient is dealing with loneliness and money troubles after losing their partner. What do these life events represent?

options.A: Genetic and chromosomal mutations
options.B: Environmental and situational stressors
options.C: Primary endocrine abnormalities
options.D: Congenital brain structural defects

explanation: You nailed it! Things happening in a person's surroundings—like loss, isolation, or financial stress—are situational triggers that can spark depression. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why do nurses use standard screening tools like the Patient Health Questionnaire in clinical practice?

options.A: To quantify and measure depression symptom severity
options.B: To measure blood levels of neurotransmitters
options.C: To test physical strength and muscular endurance
options.D: To diagnose specific neurological brain disorders

explanation: Exactly! Screening tools give us a clear, structured way to score how severe a patient's depressive symptoms are so we can track their progress. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why should nurses actively ask patients about their mood instead of waiting for them to bring it up?

options.A: Patients with depression lose the ability to speak completely
options.B: Hospital policy forbids patients from mentioning sadness first
options.C: Many patients keep feelings hidden due to social stigma
options.D: Physical assessments replace the need for verbal interviews

explanation: Spot on! Because society often judges mental health issues, many patients hide their pain. Asking gently and directly lets them know it's safe to talk. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h4)

question: A depressed patient says that life feels completely hopeless. What is the best, most therapeutic way to reply?

options.A: It sounds like you are carrying a very heavy burden right now. Let us talk about it.
options.B: Do not worry about it, many people feel much worse than you do.
options.C: Everything will look much brighter tomorrow once you get some sleep.
options.D: You have so many things to be grateful for, so try not to feel down.

explanation: Wonderful! Validating their feelings without dismissing them builds trust and opens the door for a truly helpful conversation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is it helpful to encourage small, manageable daily goals for a patient struggling with severe depression?

options.A: It prevents the patient from feeling overwhelmed by large tasks
options.B: It eliminates the need for any prescribed medication
options.C: It guarantees the patient will return to work immediately
options.D: It cures the chemical imbalance in the brain instantly

explanation: You got it! Depression drains energy. Breaking the day into tiny, doable steps helps patients feel a sense of success without crashing from exhaustion. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h5)

question: About how long does it usually take for antidepressant medications to start showing noticeable improvements?

options.A: Two to four weeks
options.B: A few minutes
options.C: Twenty-four hours
options.D: Six months

explanation: Correct! Antidepressants take time to build up in the body. Patients usually need to wait two to four weeks before feeling the real benefits. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why must nurses remind patients never to stop taking their antidepressants all of a sudden?

options.A: Abrupt discontinuation instantly cures the chemical imbalance
options.B: Stopping quickly causes immediate permanent brain damage
options.C: Sudden cessation can trigger withdrawal symptoms and a return of depression
options.D: Patients will develop a physical addiction to the medication

explanation: Spot on! Stopping suddenly can cause uncomfortable withdrawal effects and bring the depression rushing back. Medication always needs to be tapered off safely under medical guidance. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the most important nursing action when a patient talks about active thoughts of suicide?

options.A: Wait until the next scheduled clinic visit to report it
options.B: Leave the patient alone in a quiet room to reflect
options.C: Maintain constant supervision and provide a safe environment
options.D: Tell the patient to distract themselves with a hobby

explanation: You nailed it! Safety is always priority number one. Keeping a close eye on the patient and removing any hazards keeps them safe during a crisis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h7)

question: Which of these statements is true when it comes to asking a patient directly about suicide?

options.A: Asking directly opens the door for help and does not cause suicidal thoughts
options.B: Nurses should only ask about suicide if the patient brings it up first
options.C: Asking about suicide will plant the idea into a healthy patient's mind
options.D: Direct questioning is discouraged because it increases patient agitation

explanation: Brilliant! Asking directly doesn't put the idea in their head—it actually brings immense relief because it shows you care and understand how much pain they are in. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T2#GNS324_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary characteristic of a psychotic state?

options.A: An overwhelming physical exhaustion from chronic insomnia
options.B: A severe drop in resting blood pressure and heart rate
options.C: A temporary inability to remember recent childhood events
options.D: A profound disruption in a person's perception of reality

explanation: Psychosis fundamentally alters how an individual perceives and interacts with the world around them, often disconnecting them from shared reality. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is managing psychosis in a home setting uniquely challenging for community nurses?

options.A: Nurses must prescribe all antipsychotic drugs independently
options.B: Patients always refuse all forms of oral medication at home
options.C: Family members are legally barred from participating in care
options.D: Nurses face unpredictable environments and limited immediate backup

explanation: Community settings lack the controlled security and instant staff support found inside acute psychiatric hospital wards. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h1)

question: Hearing voices when no one is speaking around the patient is called what?

options.A: Disorganized thinking
options.B: A hallucination
options.C: A delusion
options.D: An illusion

explanation: Hallucinations involve sensory perceptions like hearing or seeing things in the absolute absence of any external environmental stimuli. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h2)

question: Why should a nurse avoid arguing against a patient's firmly held persecutory delusion?

options.A: It is illegal for healthcare workers to question psychiatric symptoms
options.B: It can escalate agitation and destroy trust in the nurse-patient relationship
options.C: It will immediately cure the patient of their false beliefs
options.D: It proves to the patient that the hospital staff are part of the conspiracy

explanation: Challenging delusions directly rarely changes the patient's mind and usually causes defensiveness, anger, and a breakdown in therapeutic rapport. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which neurotransmitter is most heavily implicated in the development of positive psychotic symptoms?

options.A: Serotonin
options.B: Norepinephrine
options.C: Dopamine
options.D: Acetylcholine

explanation: Excess or hyperactivity of dopamine transmission in specific brain pathways is a primary neurochemical factor linked to psychosis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h3)

question: A young adult client presents with sudden acute psychosis after heavy use of psychoactive substances. What should the nurse suspect as a primary trigger?

options.A: An acute vitamin deficiency caused by poor meal choices
options.B: Substance-induced psychotic disorder from drug exposure
options.C: A permanent neurodegenerative disease of old age
options.D: A normal physiological reaction to physical exercise

explanation: Psychoactive substances are well-known triggers that can induce acute psychotic symptoms in vulnerable individuals within community settings. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing a Mental Status Examination during a home visit?

options.A: To test the patient's long-term memory from primary school days
options.B: To diagnose infectious diseases present in the home environment
options.C: To evaluate the patient's current cognitive and psychological functioning
options.D: To measure the exact weight loss caused by poor nutrition

explanation: The MSE provides a structured snapshot of a patient's mental state at the exact time of the clinical evaluation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why is environmental safety assessment particularly crucial when visiting a home psychiatric client?

options.A: Community nurses are required to clean and tidy the patient's living room
options.B: Unpredictable behavior combined with accessible weapons increases immediate risk
options.C: Houses in urban areas lack proper ventilation for psychiatric drugs
options.D: Family members often hide all furniture to protest medical care

explanation: Assessing for potential weapons or hazards helps the nurse prevent physical harm during unpredictable shifts in the patient's mental state. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which medication class is most commonly associated with extrapyramidal side effects like muscle stiffness?

options.A: H2 receptor antagonists
options.B: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.C: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.D: First-generation antipsychotics

explanation: Typical or first-generation antipsychotics have a strong affinity for blocking dopamine receptors, frequently triggering extrapyramidal side effects. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of long-acting injectable antipsychotics for community-dwelling clients?

options.A: They cure the underlying genetic cause of schizophrenia permanently
options.B: They allow family members to administer injections without training
options.C: They completely eliminate all possible side effects of the medication
options.D: They improve adherence by removing the need for daily pill-taking

explanation: Injectable depot medications release slowly over weeks, solving the major challenge of daily oral medication refusal or forgetfulness. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h5)

question: Which action is recommended when verbally de-escalating an agitated client at home?

options.A: Maintain a loud, commanding voice to assert absolute authority
options.B: Stare directly and continuously into the patient's eyes to show dominance
options.C: Corner the patient gently to prevent them from moving around
options.D: Speak in a calm, low tone using short and simple sentences

explanation: Calm, simple communication reduces sensory overload and helps lower anxiety and agitation in an upset client. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h6)

question: What should a community nurse do immediately if verbal de-escalation fails and physical violence is imminent?

options.A: Withdraw immediately from the home and call for emergency assistance
options.B: Attempt to physically restrain the patient alone using hospital holds
options.C: Argue louder to prove that the patient is acting incorrectly
options.D: Lock all exterior doors from the inside to trap the patient

explanation: Nurse safety is always the top priority; when violence becomes unavoidable in an unsecure home setting, immediate evacuation and professional backup are required. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is a common consequence experienced by family members caring for a relative with chronic psychosis?

options.A: Immediate immunity to psychological stress
options.B: Caregiver burnout and emotional exhaustion
options.C: Enhanced physical strength from heavy lifting
options.D: Complete financial independence from local markets

explanation: The continuous demands of managing severe mental illness at home often lead to profound fatigue and psychological burnout in family caregivers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h7)

question: Why is teaching families to spot early warning signs of relapse so important?

options.A: It replaces the need for any future visits from community nurses
options.B: It enables early intervention that can prevent a full-blown psychotic crisis
options.C: It allows families to punish the patient before symptoms worsen
options.D: It proves that the patient is faking illness to gain attention

explanation: Catching subtle behavioral changes early allows for prompt medical adjustment before the patient deteriorates into an acute emergency. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h7)

question: What does a comprehensive recovery approach for a client with psychosis primarily focus on?

options.A: Restoring social skills, daily independence, and a meaningful life
options.B: Ensuring the patient never speaks to family members or friends again
options.C: Keeping the patient permanently locked inside their home away from society
options.D: Focusing solely on medication without addressing social or life goals

explanation: Recovery in mental health encompasses personal growth, social reconnection, and functioning well, not just the absence of clinical symptoms. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h8)

question: When is the best time for a nurse to collaborate with a client to create a written relapse prevention plan?

options.A: Only after the patient has experienced three consecutive relapses
options.B: When the patient is calm, stable, and able to think clearly
options.C: Immediately after discharging the patient from nursing school
options.D: During an active, violent psychotic episode in the emergency room

explanation: Collaborative planning requires cognitive clarity and stability, making periods of wellness the ideal time to map out future crisis responses. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T3#GNS324_U4_T3_h8)

question: What primary body system is affected by cerebral palsy?

options.A: Peripheral nervous system
options.B: Respiratory system
options.C: Central nervous system
options.D: Cardiovascular system

explanation: Cerebral palsy originates from non-progressive brain lesions affecting motor control centers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is cerebral palsy classified as a non-progressive disorder?

options.A: Motor skills improve without any medical intervention
options.B: The initial brain injury does not worsen over time
options.C: Symptoms completely disappear by adulthood
options.D: Treatment completely repairs damaged brain tissue

explanation: The term non-progressive means the original injury to the brain remains stable, even though physical symptoms can change as the child develops. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: A common perinatal cause of cerebral palsy is...

options.A: iron deficiency anemia
options.B: childhood asthma
options.C: birth asphyxia
options.D: congenital heart defect

explanation: Lack of oxygen during the birth process damages developing motor pathways in the infant brain. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which factor represents a postnatal risk for developing cerebral palsy?

options.A: Premature birth at 28 weeks
options.B: Bacterial meningitis in infancy
options.C: Maternal gestational diabetes
options.D: Severe placental abruption

explanation: Infections affecting the central nervous system after birth can cause permanent neurological damage leading to cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h2)

question: The most common clinical type of cerebral palsy is...

options.A: dyskinetic
options.B: ataxic
options.C: spastic
options.D: mixed

explanation: Spastic cerebral palsy accounts for the majority of cases, presenting with tight muscles and increased tone. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: Damage to the cerebellum in cerebral palsy typically leads to which clinical feature?

options.A: Rigid, unyielding muscle stiffness
options.B: Persistent asymmetrical tonic neck reflex
options.C: Poor balance and uncoordinated movements
options.D: Slow, writhing involuntary movements

explanation: The cerebellum coordinates balance and smooth movement, so injury here results in ataxic features. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: A primary clinical indicator of cerebral palsy in an infant is...

options.A: excessive linear growth
options.B: early loss of primary teeth
options.C: delayed motor milestones
options.D: premature puberty

explanation: Delays in sitting, rolling, and walking are often the earliest signs noticed by parents and healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is a common clinical finding during physical examination of an infant with spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Hyperactive immune response to standard vaccines
options.B: Flaccid muscle tone throughout all extremities
options.C: Rapid acquisition of fine pincer grasp skills
options.D: Persistent primitive reflexes past the normal age

explanation: Normal infant reflexes should fade as the nervous system matures, but they persist longer in children with cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is most useful for identifying structural brain lesions in cerebral palsy?

options.A: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.B: Bone density scan
options.C: Abdominal ultrasound
options.D: Standard chest radiograph

explanation: MRI provides detailed images of brain tissue, helping clinicians pinpoint areas of injury or developmental malformation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h5)

question: A nurse assessing a child with suspected cerebral palsy should prioritize evaluating which parameter?

options.A: Liver enzymes and clotting factors
options.B: Muscle tone and developmental milestones
options.C: Blood glucose and electrolyte balance
options.D: Cardiac rhythm and peripheral pulses

explanation: Because cerebral palsy primarily affects movement and posture, evaluating tone and milestone progress is the core assessment priority. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h5)

question: The main goal of physiotherapy in managing cerebral palsy is to...

options.A: cure the underlying brain lesion permanently
options.B: stimulate rapid cognitive development
options.C: replace the need for surgical intervention
options.D: prevent contractures and maintain mobility

explanation: Regular stretching and movement exercises help keep joints flexible and prevent shortening of muscles. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why is an interprofessional team necessary for the care of a child with cerebral palsy?

options.A: Hospital policy mandates multiple specialists for all pediatric disorders
options.B: The condition affects multiple body systems and developmental domains
options.C: Physicians cannot prescribe medications without therapist approval
options.D: Therapists take over total nursing responsibilities at home

explanation: Cerebral palsy impacts movement, communication, nutrition, and growth, requiring diverse expertise for comprehensive management. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: A key psychosocial nursing intervention for parents of a child with cerebral palsy is...

options.A: advising them to limit family visits
options.B: suggesting institutional placement immediately
options.C: discouraging questions about prognosis
options.D: connecting them with parent support groups

explanation: Support groups offer shared experiences and emotional backing, helping families cope with the challenges of long-term care. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of nurse-led education regarding home positioning?

options.A: Accelerating linear growth velocity in infancy
options.B: Preventing joint contractures and skin breakdown
options.C: Enhancing visual acuity in dim lighting
options.D: Eliminating the need for physical therapy

explanation: Proper positioning distributes pressure evenly and keeps limbs aligned, reducing the risk of deformities and pressure ulcers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h7)

question: Which physical complication is commonly associated with long-term spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Joint contractures
options.C: Chronic kidney stones
options.D: Type 2 diabetes mellitus

explanation: Persistent muscle tightness over time leads to permanent shortening of muscles and tendons around joints. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h8)

question: What factor most heavily influences the long-term prognosis for independent living in cerebral palsy?

options.A: Birth weight regardless of subsequent medical complications
options.B: Geographic location of the family residence
options.C: Type of formula fed to the infant during the first year
options.D: Severity of motor impairment and associated cognitive function

explanation: Children with milder motor involvement and normal intellect have a higher potential for independent adult functioning. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h8)

question: What core area of development is primarily affected in Autism Spectrum Disorder?

options.A: Social communication and interaction
options.B: Long-term memory retention
options.C: Skeletal muscle strength
options.D: Gross motor skill coordination

explanation: Autism Spectrum Disorder fundamentally impacts how a person communicates and interacts socially with others. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h1)

question: A toddler who does not respond to their name or point to objects is showing early signs of what condition?

options.A: Autism Spectrum Disorder
options.B: Obsessive compulsive disorder
options.C: Conduct disorder
options.D: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

explanation: Missing early social milestones like responding to a name or pointing are classic early warning signs of autism. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which factor contributes most significantly to the development of autism?

options.A: Poor childhood nutrition
options.B: Genetic and environmental influences
options.C: Lack of maternal affection
options.D: Childhood vaccinations

explanation: Current medical evidence points to a complex mix of genetic predispositions and environmental risk factors. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why is autism referred to as a neurodevelopmental condition?

options.A: It involves atypical growth and development of the brain
options.B: It originates from a temporary vitamin deficiency
options.C: It stems from a primary muscle weakness
options.D: It is caused by a sudden infection in adulthood

explanation: Neurodevelopmental conditions arise from differences in how the central nervous system and brain develop over time. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h2)

question: What tool is commonly used to screen toddlers for autism during routine visits?

options.A: M-CHAT
options.B: APGAR score
options.C: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.D: Braden scale

explanation: The Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers is widely utilized by primary care providers to screen young children. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h3)

question: How is a formal diagnosis of autism typically established?

options.A: Through behavioral observation and structured clinical interviews
options.B: By measuring hormone levels in a blood sample
options.C: Using a routine chest X-ray and urinalysis
options.D: Through genetic testing of liver enzymes

explanation: Clinicians diagnose autism by observing behavior and gathering detailed developmental histories from caregivers. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which professional primarily helps an autistic patient manage sensory processing difficulties?

options.A: Physical therapist
options.B: Respiratory therapist
options.C: Occupational therapist
options.D: Pharmacist

explanation: Occupational therapists specialize in helping individuals manage sensory challenges and perform daily life activities. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h4)

question: A hospitalized autistic child shows signs of extreme sensory overload. What nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Restraining the child immediately for safety
options.B: Speaking in a loud voice to gain attention
options.C: Dimming the lights and reducing room noise
options.D: Leaving the child alone in a bright hallway

explanation: Reducing environmental stimuli helps calm an autistic patient experiencing sensory overload and prevents meltdowns. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T5#GNS324_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why are predictable routines and visual schedules beneficial in the home environment?

explanation: Brilliant! Palliative care is all about comforting patients, easing pain, and giving them dignity when curing is no longer possible. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T12#GNS324_U5_T12_h8)

question: What is the purpose of an advance care directive in nursing practice?

options.A: To state a resident's medical treatment preferences before they lose decision-making capacity
options.B: To outline the daily cleaning schedule for the resident's private room
options.C: To mandate immediate emergency surgery for all sudden health crises
options.D: To authorize the nursing staff to make financial investments on behalf of the family

explanation: Correct! An advance directive lets patients clearly state what medical treatments they want or do not want before they become unable to decide. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T12#GNS324_U5_T12_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a geriatric home?

options.A: Providing residential and specialized care for older adults
options.B: Providing vocational training programs for retired civil servants
options.C: Serving as a permanent replacement for acute care hospitals
options.D: Offering temporary shelter exclusively for discharged psychiatric patients

explanation: Geriatric homes offer structured residential and health support for older adults who can no longer live completely independently. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h1)

question: Why are residential care homes for older adults becoming more common in Nigeria?

options.A: Government policy now makes home care illegal for citizens over sixty
options.B: Traditional family support systems face growing economic and social strains
options.C: Younger generations completely reject living with their parents
options.D: Hospitals refuse to discharge elderly patients back to their families

explanation: Shifting economic conditions and urbanization mean extended families are sometimes less able to provide round-the-clock care. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h1)

question: Which of these is a major responsibility of the nurse in a geriatric home?

options.A: Personally funding all facility medical equipment purchases
options.B: Making final legal decisions regarding resident financial estates
options.C: Coordinating care plans and monitoring daily health status
options.D: Replacing attending physicians during surgical procedures

explanation: Nurses play a key role in tracking resident health and bringing together different aspects of daily care. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h2)

question: Why is noticing early behavioral changes so important for geriatric nurses?

options.A: It determines the exact monthly facility billing rate
options.B: It is required before discharging residents to their families
options.C: It prevents nurses from having to document daily shift reports
options.D: It helps spot early signs of infections or confusion

explanation: Older adults often show signs of illness like urinary tract infections through sudden confusion rather than classic pain. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h2)

question: What does the term IADL stand for in nursing assessments?

options.A: Instrumental Activities of Daily Living
options.B: Immediate Action for Dependent Living
options.C: Integrated Age-Deficit Locomotion Scale
options.D: Internal Assessment of Daily Limitations

explanation: IADLs are more complex tasks needed for independent living, such as shopping, cooking, and handling money. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h3)

question: A resident struggles to manage money and take medications on time, but eats and bathes independently. What does this point to?

options.A: Basic Activities of Daily Living deficit
options.B: Gross motor skill coordination failure
options.C: Primary cognitive functioning only
options.D: Instrumental Activities of Daily Living deficit

explanation: Handling finances and medications are Instrumental Activities of Daily Living, which usually become difficult before basic self-care tasks do. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h3)

question: What is the term for the age-related loss of muscle mass that can lead to falls?

options.A: Osteoporosis
options.B: Myopathy
options.C: Arthralgia
options.D: Sarcopenia

explanation: Sarcopenia is the natural, gradual loss of muscle mass and strength that happens as people age. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h4)

question: Why can blood pressure medications increase the risk of falls in older adults?

options.A: They directly cause severe bone softening within hours
options.B: They blur the resident's central vision permanently
options.C: They cause immediate paralysis of the lower extremities
options.D: They can cause dizziness and a sudden drop in blood pressure when standing

explanation: Blood pressure drugs can lower pressure too quickly when changing positions, causing lightheadedness and unsteadiness. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h4)

question: How is polypharmacy defined?

options.A: The practice of buying drugs from multiple different pharmacies
options.B: The wholesale manufacturing of herbal remedies in a facility
options.C: The use of multiple medications at the same time by a patient
options.D: The total prohibition of prescription drugs in old age

explanation: Polypharmacy simply means taking many medications at once, which is common when older adults manage several chronic conditions. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h5)

question: What is a major nursing concern regarding polypharmacy in older adults?

options.A: Higher risk of drug interactions and side effects
options.B: Guaranteed improvement in overall physical mobility
options.C: Elimination of all chronic disease symptoms
options.D: Reduced need for nurse supervision during medication rounds

explanation: Taking many drugs together increases the chance of negative drug interactions and toxic side effects in aging bodies. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h5)

question: What is the medical term for difficulty in swallowing?

options.A: Dyspepsia
options.B: Dysphagia
options.C: Dyspnea
options.D: Dysphasia

explanation: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, which puts older adults at risk of choking and chest infections. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h6)

question: Why are older adults in care homes often at a higher risk of dehydration?

options.A: They are legally restricted from drinking water after afternoon meals
options.B: Their kidneys completely stop producing urine as they age
options.C: Facilities intentionally withhold fluids to reduce laundry loads
options.D: They experience a weaker sense of thirst and lower body water content

explanation: Aging changes how the body handles thirst, making older individuals less likely to feel thirsty and drink enough water. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h6)

question: What is the main focus of palliative care?

options.A: Isolating the resident from family members to prevent grief
options.B: Maximizing comfort and quality of life for serious illnesses
options.C: Accelerating the natural dying process through active euthanasia
options.D: Finding a permanent cure for chronic neurodegenerative diseases

explanation: Palliative care centers on relieving pain and managing distressing symptoms to ensure dignity and comfort. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h7)

question: Which of these is an important nursing duty during end-of-life care?

options.A: Transferring the dying resident immediately to an emergency ward
options.B: Supporting both the resident and their family with compassionate communication
options.C: Forcing the resident to consume high-calorie meals against their will
options.D: Stopping all forms of pain relief to keep the patient alert

explanation: Good end-of-life care involves addressing the emotional and spiritual needs of both the patient and their loved ones. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h7)

question: Which body regulates nursing practice and professional standards in Nigeria?

options.A: Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs
options.B: Nigerian Union of Pensioners
options.C: West African Medical Association
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: The NMCN is the statutory organization responsible for regulating nursing education and practice in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h8)

question: Why are regular quality checks necessary in geriatric facilities?

options.A: To prove that residents no longer require any medical supervision
options.B: To ensure that clinical care, hygiene, and safety protocols meet proper standards
options.C: To eliminate the need for any documentation by floor nurses
options.D: To give administrators an excuse to reduce staff salaries annually

explanation: Audits help maintain high standards of care, protect vulnerable residents, and ensure continuous improvement in the facility. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T13#GNS324_U5_T13_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of care in a hospice home facility?

options.A: Providing comfort and improving quality of life
options.B: Administering aggressive curative medical treatments
options.C: Conducting clinical research trials for terminal diseases
options.D: Rehabilitating patients to return to independent living

explanation: Hospice care shifts away from curing the disease and concentrates entirely on comfort measures and quality of remaining life. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h1)

question: A patient is considered eligible for admission to a hospice facility when their life expectancy is approximately how long?

options.A: One to two years
options.B: Five years or more
options.C: Six months or less
options.D: Less than one month

explanation: Standard admission guidelines require a physician certification that the terminal illness has a prognosis of six months or less. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h1)

question: How does the palliative care philosophy view the dying process?

options.A: As an unpredictable event that requires isolation
options.B: As a condition that can be reversed with therapy
options.C: As a natural part of the human life cycle
options.D: As a medical failure that must be fought

explanation: Palliative philosophy accepts death as a natural transition and focuses on comfort rather than artificial prolongation of life. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h2)

question: A family insists on starting invasive feeding tubes for a terminal patient in pain. What action best reflects palliative philosophy?

options.A: Discussing comfort goals and the burden of invasive procedures with the family
options.B: Ignoring the family and following only the primary doctor's standing orders
options.C: Immediately starting the feeding tubes to satisfy the family's anxiety
options.D: Discharging the patient due to non-compliance with the care plan

explanation: Palliative care relies on communication to help families understand that invasive interventions may increase discomfort without extending meaningful life. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h2)

question: Which professional on the hospice team primarily helps families manage financial and emotional logistics?

options.A: Medical social worker
options.B: Hospital pharmacist
options.C: Staff physical therapist
options.D: Attending physician

explanation: Social workers are trained to assist families with counseling, financial resources, and navigating complex healthcare logistics. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h3)

question: Why is an interdisciplinary team essential in a hospice home facility?

options.A: Patients have complex physical, emotional, and spiritual needs that one discipline cannot meet alone
options.B: Hospital regulations strictly mandate a minimum staff count for every shift
options.C: Nurses prefer to delegate all patient assessment duties to trained volunteers
options.D: Doctors refuse to communicate directly with family members in home settings

explanation: End-of-life care touches every aspect of a person's well-being, requiring specialized input from nursing, medicine, social work, and spiritual care. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h3)

question: What is the preferred scheduling method for administering pain medication in hospice care?

options.A: Only when the patient cries
options.B: Around-the-clock schedule
options.C: Every time vitals are checked
options.D: Strictly during morning shifts

explanation: Scheduled dosing prevents pain from returning, maintaining steady comfort rather than chasing pain after it peaks. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h4)

question: A non-communicative terminal patient grimaces and pulls away during repositioning. What does this behavior indicate?

options.A: The patient is reacting to a pleasant sensory stimulus
options.B: The patient is attempting to stand up independently
options.C: The patient is experiencing pain and needs comfort assessment
options.D: The patient is having a normal muscle spasm without discomfort

explanation: Facial grimacing and withdrawal are reliable behavioral pain indicators for patients who cannot verbally report discomfort. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h4)

question: What type of grief do family members experience before the actual death of their loved one?

options.A: Complicated grief
options.B: Unresolved trauma
options.C: Pathological mourning
options.D: Anticipatory grief

explanation: Grief that occurs before a predicted loss as families process the impending death is known as anticipatory grief. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h5)

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates psychosocial support for a dying patient expressing deep fear?

options.A: Explaining all the hospital administrative policies in detail
options.B: Sitting quietly by the bed and listening attentively to their concerns
options.C: Changing the subject to something cheerful to lift their mood
options.D: Administering a high dose of sedative medication immediately

explanation: Presence and active listening validate the patient's emotional pain and reduce feelings of isolation during end-of-life stages. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h5)

question: Which legal document designates a specific person to make medical decisions if the patient becomes incapacitated?

options.A: Durable power of attorney for healthcare
options.B: General financial asset trust
options.C: Primary physician care contract
options.D: Facility admission discharge form

explanation: A healthcare proxy or durable power of attorney legally empowers a chosen surrogate to speak on the patient's behalf. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h6)

question: What is the primary responsibility of the nurse when a family's cultural death rituals conflict with standard facility routines?

options.A: Strictly enforce hospital routines to maintain operational order
options.B: Report the family to local authorities for unusual customs
options.C: Refuse care and ask the family to leave the facility
options.D: Accommodate the cultural practices safely whenever possible

explanation: Nurses must respect cultural diversity and adapt care routines to support meaningful traditions surrounding death. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h6)

question: How long do hospice bereavement services typically continue after a patient passes away?

options.A: Only until the funeral concludes
options.B: Exactly forty-eight hours
options.C: Several months to a year
options.D: Until the final medical bill is paid

explanation: Standard hospice programs provide bereavement follow-up and support for at least twelve months following a loss. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h7)

question: What is the main purpose of post-death bereavement follow-up by the hospice team?

options.A: To inspect the family home for cleanliness and safety hazards
options.B: To collect remaining financial fees for the room accommodation
options.C: To help surviving family members process grief and adjust to their loss
options.D: To recruit family members to work as voluntary facility staff

explanation: Bereavement support assists families through the difficult transition of mourning and monitors for signs of complicated grief. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of maternity homes in local Nigerian communities?

options.A: To conduct medical research on tropical diseases
options.B: To bridge healthcare gaps by providing close maternal care
options.C: To replace federal teaching hospitals entirely for all surgeries
options.D: To manufacture essential obstetric drugs locally

explanation: Maternity homes bring essential maternal and newborn health services closer to grassroots populations who lack easy access to large hospitals. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h1)

question: Why is nurse-led care in maternity homes particularly valuable in resource-limited settings?

options.A: It guarantees that surgical interventions are performed on site
options.B: It reduces the cost of medical equipment maintenance to zero
options.C: It offers continuous and personalized support for normal pregnancies
options.D: It eliminates the need for any subsequent hospital referrals

explanation: Nurses and midwives provide close, individual attention that supports normal physiological birth and early detection of complications. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h1)

question: Which regulatory body licenses midwives and nurses to practice in Nigeria?

options.A: West African Health Organization
options.B: Pharmacists Council of Nigeria
options.C: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.D: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria

explanation: The NMCN is the statutory body responsible for regulating the nursing and midwifery profession in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h2)

question: A maternity home owner fails to maintain proper delivery registers. What regulatory consequence is likely?

options.A: Suspension or revocation of the operating license
options.B: Immediate promotion to a federal health board
options.C: Automatic upgrade to a secondary hospital
options.D: Exemption from annual tax obligations

explanation: Failure to maintain statutory records violates licensing conditions, leading to disciplinary actions and facility closure. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h2)

question: A pregnant woman with a previous cesarean section registers at a primary maternity home. What is the correct action?

options.A: Plan for a trial of labor with standard oxytocin augmentation
options.B: Refer her promptly to a facility with surgical capabilities
options.C: Perform a routine ultrasound and discharge her until term
options.D: Manage her exclusively with herbal remedies at home

explanation: Previous uterine scars present a high risk of rupture, which exceeds the scope of practice for a basic maternity home. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h3)

question: What primary clinical boundary defines the practice scope of a standard maternity home?

options.A: Treatment of chronic medical conditions like diabetes
options.B: Management of complex neonatal congenital anomalies
options.C: Performance of elective and emergency cesarean sections
options.D: Management of strictly low-risk, uncomplicated pregnancies and births

explanation: Maternity homes are designed for normal, low-risk physiological childbearing processes. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h3)

question: What is a core component of routine antenatal assessment in a maternity home?

options.A: Routine pelvic floor reconstructive surgery
options.B: Magnetic resonance imaging of the fetus
options.C: Blood pressure measurement and urinalysis
options.D: Daily blood glucose tolerance testing

explanation: Checking blood pressure and urine protein helps detect early signs of pre-eclampsia during antenatal visits. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h4)

question: A primigravida at 32 weeks gestation presents with persistent frontal headaches and pedal edema. What should the midwife do first?

options.A: Book her for a routine follow-up visit in four weeks
options.B: Tell her to go home and rest with her feet elevated
options.C: Prescribe strong analgesics for pain relief
options.D: Check her blood pressure and test her urine immediately

explanation: Headaches and edema in pregnancy are classic warning signs of pre-eclampsia that require immediate screening. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h4)

question: Which clinical tool is mandatory for monitoring the progress of active labor?

options.A: Partograph
options.B: Spirometer
options.C: Otoscope
options.D: Electrocardiogram

explanation: The partograph provides a pictorial overview of labor progress and helps detect prolonged labor early. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h5)

question: Why is plotting progress on a partograph critical in a maternity home setting?

options.A: It serves as a legal prescription chart for administering antibiotics
options.B: It replaces the need for listening to the fetal heart rate
options.C: It automatically stops postpartum hemorrhage from occurring
options.D: It gives an early warning when labor deviates from the normal curve

explanation: Crossing action or alert lines on the partograph indicates that labor is not progressing normally, prompting timely action. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for close observation during the first two hours after delivery?

options.A: Assessing the mother's ability to walk unassisted
options.B: Initiating immediate postnatal family planning surgery
options.C: Prevention and early detection of postpartum hemorrhage
options.D: Monitoring maternal recovery from general anesthesia

explanation: Most cases of primary postpartum hemorrhage occur within the immediate postpartum period, requiring intense vigilance. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h6)

question: Why is drying and wrapping a newborn baby an immediate priority after birth?

options.A: To prevent the development of neonatal jaundice
options.B: To stimulate the kidneys to produce urine
options.C: To prevent rapid heat loss and neonatal hypothermia
options.D: To close the ductus arteriosus in the heart

explanation: Wet newborns lose heat quickly through evaporation, making prompt drying and thermal care vital for survival. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h6)

question: What is the frontline medication used to manage eclamptic seizures in a maternity home?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate
options.B: Diazepam infusion
options.C: Oxytocin injection
options.D: Hydralazine tablets

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for preventing and treating convulsions associated with severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h7)

question: A woman bleeds heavily immediately after delivering the placenta, and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What initial action should the midwife take?

options.A: Send the patient home for complete bed rest
options.B: Wait for laboratory results before acting
options.C: Administer oral iron supplements
options.D: Perform immediate bimanual uterine massage

explanation: A boggy uterus indicates uterine atony; massaging it stimulates contraction to constrict bleeding vessels. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h7)

question: Why is sending a comprehensive referral note along with an emergency patient crucial?

options.A: It serves as a formal bill for services rendered at the home
options.B: It eliminates the need for any further clinical examination
options.C: It informs the receiving team of interventions already performed
options.D: It guarantees free treatment at the secondary hospital

explanation: A clear referral note provides vital history, vital signs, and medications given, preventing treatment delays and duplication. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h8)

question: Which factor represents a major avoidable delay in maternal mortality during emergencies?

options.A: Too many well-equipped hospitals in rural areas
options.B: Delays in recognizing danger signs and arranging transport
options.C: Excessive availability of ambulance services
options.D: Early arrival of patients at primary health centers

explanation: The three delays model highlights that delayed recognition and transport are major contributors to maternal deaths. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h8)

question: What is the most effective single method for preventing the spread of infections in a maternity home?

options.A: Using scented disinfectants on floors
options.B: Regular and thorough hand hygiene
options.C: Painting facility walls with bright colors
options.D: Wearing heavy leather aprons during delivery

explanation: Proper hand hygiene remains the single most effective way to interrupt the transmission of infectious pathogens. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h9)

question: How should used surgical blades and needles be disposed of after a delivery?

options.A: Washed in the sink and stored for future use
options.B: Recapped carefully by hand and thrown in a dustbin
options.C: Burned in an open pit behind the maternity ward
options.D: Placed immediately into a puncture-resistant safety box

explanation: Sharps must be disposed of in designated safety boxes without recapping to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T15#GNS324_U5_T15_h9)

question: What is the primary focus of long-term care compared to acute care?

options.A: Maintaining function and quality of life over time
options.B: Treating sudden infectious diseases in isolation units
options.C: Achieving rapid cure and immediate physical stabilization
options.D: Providing short-term rehabilitation after minor surgeries

explanation: Long-term care centers on chronic support and managing daily living needs rather than seeking a short-term cure for acute illnesses. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why is preserving autonomy a core objective in long-term care facilities?

options.A: It reduces the total number of nursing staff required on duty
options.B: It completely eliminates the risk of accidental resident falls
options.C: It empowers residents to retain personal dignity and control
options.D: It speeds up the healing process of acute surgical wounds

explanation: Allowing residents to make choices about their daily routines promotes psychological well-being and preserves their sense of self. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which group forms the largest demographic residing in long-term care facilities?

options.A: Older adults with multiple chronic conditions
options.B: Children with congenital heart defects
options.C: Adults recovering from acute respiratory infections
options.D: Younger adults with traumatic brain injuries

explanation: Older adults make up the vast majority of long-term care residents due to age-related frailty and chronic illness. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h2)

question: A resident with advanced Alzheimer's disease is admitted. What primary environment should the nurse expect?

options.A: A secure unit with specialized behavioral management support
options.B: A high-dependency unit for continuous mechanical ventilation
options.C: An open acute medical ward with frequent vital sign checks
options.D: An outpatient clinic focused on rapid physical rehabilitation

explanation: Dementia patients require safe, secure environments and structured care tailored to manage cognitive deficits and wandering behaviors. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h2)

question: How does nursing assessment in long-term care differ from acute care?

options.A: It is performed only once upon the initial admission of the client
options.B: It is an ongoing, continuous process tracking gradual baseline shifts
options.C: It ignores psychosocial history in favor of strict lab values
options.D: It focuses exclusively on diagnosing sudden surgical complications

explanation: Because residents live in the facility long-term, assessments must continually monitor subtle changes over extended periods. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of establishing accurate baseline data for a long-term care resident?

options.A: Ensuring the resident never requires transfer to an acute hospital
options.B: Reducing the frequency of mandatory physician medication reviews
options.C: Distinguishing between chronic baselines and acute health changes
options.D: Eliminating the need for periodic functional reassessments

explanation: Knowing a resident's normal baseline helps nurses quickly recognize when an actual acute medical deterioration is occurring. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h3)

question: What is the core philosophy of person-centered care in long-term facilities?

options.A: Prioritizing staff convenience over individual resident routines
options.B: Delegating all care planning decisions entirely to attending physicians
options.C: Centering care around the resident's personal preferences and habits
options.D: Enforcing strict institutional schedules for all residents equally

explanation: Person-centered care respects individual choices and tailors routines to fit the resident's lifelong habits and desires. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h4)

question: How does involving residents in their care planning directly affect clinical outcomes?

options.A: It guarantees complete physical recovery from permanent disabilities
options.B: It improves care compliance and reduces behavioral agitation
options.C: It removes the need for nursing documentation of daily care
options.D: It completely halts the natural progression of chronic diseases

explanation: When residents feel heard and respected through personalized care, they experience less frustration and cooperate better with daily routines. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which of the following represents an Activity of Daily Living (ADL)?

options.A: Shopping
options.B: Feeding
options.C: Managing finances
options.D: Cooking

explanation: Feeding, bathing, dressing, and toileting are classic Activities of Daily Living, whereas cooking and shopping are Instrumental ADLs. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h5)

question: A resident with mild stroke weakness struggles to hold a standard spoon during lunch. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Withhold the meal until the resident regains full hand strength
options.B: Feed the entire meal quickly to ensure adequate nutrition
options.C: Wait until a family member arrives to assist with feeding
options.D: Provide an adaptive utensil to encourage independent eating

explanation: Using adaptive devices supports remaining functional ability and encourages independence during self-care tasks. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse within the interprofessional long-term care team?

options.A: Performing physical therapy exercises without professional input
options.B: Exclusively managing financial planning and social advocacy
options.C: Solely prescribing and modifying all resident medication doses
options.D: Serving as the central communication hub coordinating care input

explanation: Nurses coordinate data and interventions among various team members to ensure the resident receives cohesive, holistic care. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h6)

question: A resident begins coughing frequently and pocketing food during meals. Which specialist should the nurse consult first?

options.A: Medical Social Worker
options.B: Speech-Language Pathologist
options.C: Physical Therapist
options.D: Occupational Therapist

explanation: Coughing and pocketing food during meals are classic signs of dysphagia, which falls under the expertise of a speech-language pathologist. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is a standard nursing intervention to prevent pressure injuries in immobile residents?

options.A: Keeping room temperatures exceptionally warm
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to minimize skin moisture
options.C: Repositioning the resident every two hours
options.D: Applying adhesive tape firmly over bony prominences

explanation: Regular repositioning relieves prolonged pressure on bony prominences, which is the primary mechanical cause of pressure injuries. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h7)

question: Which factor makes long-term care residents particularly susceptible to infectious disease outbreaks?

options.A: Excessive physical activity and outdoor rehabilitation
options.B: High rates of complete physical self-sufficiency
options.C: Strict adherence to solitary room isolation protocols
options.D: Communal living spaces and age-related immune decline

explanation: Living closely with others combined with weakened immune systems puts LTC residents at higher risk for contagious infections. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the purpose of an advance directive in long-term care?

options.A: Granting nurses full legal authority to modify resident financial assets
options.B: Eliminating the need for family involvement in medical decisions
options.C: Mandating aggressive life-prolonging measures in all terminal cases
options.D: Allowing individuals to state medical wishes before losing capacity

explanation: Advance directives give patients a voice in their future medical care before they become unable to make decisions. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h8)

question: How does the primary goal of care shift when a resident transitions to palliative end-of-life care?

options.A: From personalized room routines to strict institutional isolation
options.B: From chronic disease monitoring to acute surgical intervention
options.C: From curative treatment to comfort, pain control, and dignity
options.D: From daily hygiene maintenance to aggressive physical therapy

explanation: Palliative care centers on maximizing comfort and managing symptoms rather than attempting to cure underlying terminal conditions. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T2#GNS324_U5_T2_h8)

question: What is the main difference between skilled care and custodial care?

options.A: Skilled care requires licensed health professionals for complex medical needs.
options.B: Custodial care is only provided inside large acute care hospitals.
options.C: Custodial care requires advanced clinical judgment and monitoring.
options.D: Skilled care focuses exclusively on helping residents bathe and dress.

explanation: You've got this! Skilled care is all about medical tasks done by trained pros, while custodial care helps with everyday living activities like bathing. Great job keeping them straight! [learn more](GNS324_U5_T3#GNS324_U5_T3_h1)

question: Why is skilled care so important for an elderly patient just leaving the hospital?

options.A: To replace the need for any future primary care physician visits.
options.B: To prevent minor clinical changes from turning into severe health emergencies.
options.C: To ensure the patient never returns to their personal home.
options.D: To completely eliminate all forms of physical therapy.

explanation: Spotting small health changes early is what skilled nursing is all about! It keeps our patients stable and out of trouble. Well done! [learn more](GNS324_U5_T3#GNS324_U5_T3_h1)
